entries.title: Bears DT Jeffery Simmons tees off on Lions C Juice Scruggs, LG Christian Mahogany: 'Lot of crying'
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons just joined the NFC North scrum and he’s already sick of the Lions. Specifically, he doesn’t want to hear anything more from center Juice Scruggs and left guard Christian Mahogany.</p><p>In <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-draft-dream-comes-true-as-qb-caleb-williams-wr-rome-odunze-lead-39-35-win-over-lions" >the Bears’ wild 39-35 win</a> at Ford Field on Thursday, Scruggs committed three false starts and Mahogany got flagged for one as well while lining up opposite Simmons.</p><p>“It’s a lot of crying on that side of the ball when that happens,” Simmons said.</p><p>They complained, Simmons said, that he was illegally imitating quarterback Jared Goff’s snap count to get them to jump. Simmons, as he explained to the officials during the game, was only calling out to his teammates to alert them that Goff switched a play to a run, and he said that only happened once anyway.</p><p>“If your quarterback checks, I’m allowed to say, ‘He’s checking to a run,’” Simmons continued. “I said, ‘It’s a run.’ It’s not my fault that your center jumped.</p><p>“That’s literally the only time that I said something. All the other ones, [Scruggs] just knew when I lined up right over his head, that can be a little — I mean, that’s on him. He’s trying to get to a position so he can block me.”</p><p>He added, “I don’t have to cheat... But you’re going to get a lot of complaining when you lose a football game and you get a false start.”</p><p>Simmons said the official told him he was fine as long as he didn’t say anything that sounded like, “hut.” He insisted he had no intention other than to communicate with teammates.</p><p>Mahogany couldn’t leave it at that, though, and taunted Simmons after blocking him on running back Jahmyr Gibbs’ 70-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter. He got a flag for that, but he might get worse when he sees Simmons again in Week 17 at Soldier Field.</p><p>“That’s what you call a frontrunner,” Simmons said. “He’s a big frontrunner. Half the time, I wasn’t even on his side, and he was just talking.</p><p>“When we get the opportunity to attack him — we’ll see him again, I’ll tell you that. After the game, he went missing. There’s a lot of frontrunners. We’ll see him again.”</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Bears' draft dream comes true as QB Caleb Williams, WR Rome Odunze lead 39-35 win over Lions
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> and Rome Odunze dreamed of a moment like this the day they became <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> teammates. And the Bears believed those two could lead them out of the ashes.</p><p>They did it Thursday in a game against the Lions that so often looked like a lost cause. After all the harrowing twists, trailing until their final play, they were as calm as could be as Williams found Odunze in the back of the end zone with three seconds left to win 39-35.</p><p>It had been a rocky path. Williams put the team in a hole with fumble before halftime, and Odunze had been a non-factor until the final eight minutes.</p><p>Yet there they stood, celebrating a bullseye of a throw, an acrobatic catch and an improbable victory reflective of the travails they’ve endured since the Bears drafted Williams first overall and Odunze ninth in 2024 — on a stage nearby at Martius Campus Park.</p><p>“That's my guy,” Williams said. “We've been through ups, downs, all of the above. So, when those moments come up and he runs great routes, I give him the ball, he catches it.</p><p>“It just tends to go to Rome.”</p><p>It was a comeback reminiscent of last season for the Bears as they kept punching back from two-score deficits, including 35-24 with eight minutes left, and they took control of the NFC North at 9-2. It’s their best start since their 2006 Super Bowl season.</p><p>With clear command and poise, Williams took one of the most important snaps of his career on third-and-goal from the 6-yard line with nine seconds left and handled everything perfectly.</p><p>His first reads, two receivers to his left, weren’t open. The pocket closed, but he stepped up instead of scrambling. He turned to Odunze in the back, right corner of the end zone with a step on cornerback Rock Ya-Sin and lofted the ball where only he could reach it. Odunze not only made the catch, but barely got both feet down before flying out of bounds.</p><p>“It’s a difficult play,” he said casually, “but it’s in my arsenal.”</p><p>The officials scrutinized the play down to the millimeter to see if he stepped out of bounds before the catch or if he had so much as a shoelace on the line when he came down.</p><p>“Thankfully, I had the clean toes,” Odunze said.</p><p>He caught four passes, including two touchdowns, for 73 yards in the final eight minutes to finish with six for 87 overall. He’s on pace for his first 1,000-yard season.</p><p>Williams showed similar resilience on his way to completing 30 of 44 passes for a season-high 345 yards with two touchdown passes for a 106.7 passer rating, as well as running for a crucial two-point conversion to cut the Lions’ lead to 35-32 with 7:20 left.</p><p>He described his emotions on the winning touchdown pass as “nothing,” despite it obviously being one of the best victories of his career.</p><p>“We've got a job to do ... and that's part of it,” he said. “We were up and down. We regathered ourselves. We had full faith, full belief.”</p><p>Nonetheless, it was a resounding finish after struggling in the previous two games and the first half of this one.</p><p>Williams was at the center of a pivotal swing shortly before halftime that saw the Bears slip from being in position to take the lead to trailing by nine instead.</p><p>Taking the snap from his own 9-yard line, Lions defensive end Derrick Moore caught him from behind at the 2 and stripped the ball. It bounded into the end zone behind him, and right tackle Darnell Wright committed a penalty by slapping it forward.</p><p>That gave Lions coach Dan Campbell a decision with 1:07 left: Take the two points and the ball, or decline the penalty and get a prime opportunity for a touchdown from the Bears’ 14-yard line.</p><p>As he often does, Campbell gambled — and won. Quarterback Jared Goff followed with a quick scoring drive, capped by a touchdown pass to Sam LaPorta in the final seconds, to take a 19-10 lead.</p><p>With two of the NFL’s most explosive offenses battling, losing that much ground was dangerous.</p><p>The Bears’ defense struggled most of the game and allowed its season high in points, its second most yards (549) and got burned by Goff for 313 yards and touchdown and running back Jahmyr Gibbs for 205 yards rushing and three touchdowns.</p><p>But when it reached now-or-never time, the defense showed up.</p><p>Goff was at the Bears’ 34-yard line with 5:25 left and a 35-32 lead when rookie safety Dillon Thieneman caught a deflection off wide receiver Jameson Williams’ hands for an interception.</p><p>The offense failed to turn that into the go-ahead score, but the defense kept the game alive on the next possession.</p><p>Campbell went for it on fourth-and-four at the Bears’ 33-yard line hoping to close out the game, and Goff hit Gibbs in the flats with only linebacker T.J. Edwards between him and the first down. Edwards didn’t hesitate. He went straight at Gibbs’ hips and stopped him for only a yard.</p><p>“Thank God,” Simmons said. “That play right there won that football game.</p><p>“It comes down to who really wants it the most. On that fourth-down play, we wanted it more. The best running back in football, in space, that’s a hard down. He wanted it more than Gibbs on that particular play.”</p><p>The whole game felt a little like that. No matter how bleak it got for the Bears, Williams wouldn’t concede. Odunze became a role player for much of the game, but never lost interest. The defense wobbled, but never fell. Ultimately, it was just enough.</p>

entries.title: Bears win? Bears win! Bears 39, Lions 35 shouldn't have happened — wasn't going to happen — but damn sure did
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Holy cranberries, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-inactives-vs-lions-lt-theo-benedet-playing-cb-kyler-gordon-out" target="_blank" >that just happened</a>.</p><p>No wonder general manager Ryan Poles could merely pace outside the visitors’ locker room by himself, shaking his head, answering an inquiry about what he was feeling with a bemused, “Everything.”</p><p>No wonder a door cracked open and there coach Ben Johnson was, wearing a smile a mile and a half wide, his right pointer finger held high in a No. 1 sign, as he bounced in the thick locker-room air above his players, who had him on their shoulders as though they’d all just won the Super Bowl.</p><p>No wonder the Lions’ locker room was a morgue.</p><p>Somehow, Bears 39, Lions 35 happened. It shouldn’t have. It wasn’t going to, not when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> fell behind in a game — by double digits — for the first time in over six weeks, not when they flubbed a late-first-half possession for a Lions safety, not while their defense was busy <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-grades-lions-thanksgiving-nfl-caleb-williams-rome-odunze-colston-loveland-jahmyr-gibbs" target="_blank" >making Jahmyr Gibbs look like the greatest running back of all time</a>, not as the Lions kept piling up touchdowns, not after the Bears — still trailing 35-32 — came up short on fourth down with under three minutes to go.</p><p>Not with the Bears trailing throughout nearly all of yet another rough game against the Lions, who’d beaten them seven times out of eight coming in, and seemingly on the wrong end of yet another tussle in the NFC North, which in recent years has treated the Bears like doormats.</p><p>What business did linebacker T.J. Edwards have bulldogging the ultra-elusive Gibbs to the ground with an open-field tackle on fourth down to steal back the ball just as the Lions were smelling victory formation? Where did quarterback Caleb Williams and wide receiver Rome Odunze get off stunning a sea of Lions fans into Thanksgiving silence with a last-ditch touchdown connection with three seconds left — for the Lions’ maddening ninth loss in the last 10 years on what the locals must regard by now as a cursed holiday?</p><p>But they did. At 9-2, the Bears are alone in first place in what has to be the best division in football. They might not be at the level of the 49ers, reputedly the team to beat in the NFC, but they’ve thrown the Lions (8-3) for a loop, they’re a game and a half in front of the Vikings and they’re three games — count ’em — clear of the Packers, who might be one of the most dangerous last-place teams ever yet are in acute danger of missing the playoffs.</p><p>What a scene this was, during and after.</p><p>“Man, that was crazy,” wide receiver Luther Burden said. “No, I mean, that was crayyy-zy.”</p><p>“I almost can’t believe it,” offensive tackle Theo Benedet said.</p><p>Cornerback Jaylon Johnson, still in uniform, stopped by one offensive player’s locker after another’s, spreading thanks.</p><p>“Man, y’all did that,” Johnson said.</p><p>Done and done.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">TURKEY DAY DUB 🤩 <a href="https://t.co/a8fmQ3OprN">pic.twitter.com/a8fmQ3OprN</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2126083645005803522?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 26, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>TOMORROW’S HEADLINES</b></h3><p><b>The View From the Top: </b>In first place in the North at 9-2, the Bears have a great chance to go back-to-back in a wickedly good division.</p><p><b>Colston Loveland’s Injury: </b>The Bears suddenly have a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-lions-colston-loveland-carted-to-locker-room-tight-end-thursday-ford-field" >heck of a tight end problem. </a>How will this play into Ben Johnson’s offensive planning?</p><p><b>What About the Defense? </b>The win was exhilarating, but the Bears’ “D” still was (mostly) terrible. How concerning is this going forward?</p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: Bears notes: TE Colston Loveland carted off with knee injury
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Tight end Colston Loveland was quickly ruled out of Sunday’s 39-35 win against the Lions after hurting his knee in the first quarter, an ominous sign for his availability in the weeks to come.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson said after the game that he wasn’t sure of Loveland’s status and that the team planned to find out more Friday.</p><p>Loveland was hurt after being shoved backward by linebacker Trevor Nowaske and over running back D'Andre Swift at the end of a two-yard run. He sat on the back of the golf cart with a white towel over his face as he was driven to the tunnel.</p><p>Earlier in the first quarter, Loveland fumbled the ball away after being hit following a five-yard catch and run. He was hit by Lions safety Brian Branch and cornerback DJ Reed.</p><p>He entered the game with 40 catches on 60 targets for 392 yards and three touchdowns. He's spent half the season without fellow tight end Cole Kmet, who was lost for the season had knee surgery after a grisly injury against the Patriots.</p><p>“Next man up is our mentality,” quarterback Caleb Williams said. “Obviously Colston is … Colston. … And same thing with Cole. They're key parts to us in this offense.”</p><p>Rookie Sam Roush, the Bears' third tight end, caught five passes for 31 yards, while fellow. Backup Stephen Carlson had two for 30.</p><p>“[Roush] had a little hiccup there earlier in the season, and now he’s really smoothed out, and he’s only going to continue to ascend …” Johnson said “He’s become the security blanket there for our quarterback as well. We’ll see if he needs to have a bigger role here going forward.”</p><p></p><h3>Swift back</h3><p>One week after he fumbled in the fourth quarter, Swift led the Bears in both rushing and receiving, carrying the ball nine times for 65 yards and catching seven passes for 97.</p><p>Kyle Monangai had two touchown runs but gained only 15 yards on eight carries, while Salvon Ahmed gave the Bears a spark with a 46-yard rush that set up the Bears’ first points, a 40-yard field goal by Cairo Santos.</p><h3></h3><h3>Notes</h3><p>• When Jake Bates made a 24-yard field goal about three minutes into the game, he handed the Bears their first deficit since Oct. 11 in Green Bay.</p><p>• Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs ran for three touchdowns to pass former Lions star Barry Sanders, whose 52 career scores were the most in NFL history before his 25th birthday.</p><p>• Before Thursday, the Lions had won 21 home games in a row when they held the lead at halftime.</p><p>• Rap stars Wu-Tang Clan performed at halftime and got a postgame shoutout from Williams.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: How Bears coach Ben Johnson exorcized the ghost of Matt Eberflus
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — Ben Johnson’s linebackers lifted him in the air, placing one thigh atop Devin Bush’s left shoulder and the other on D’Marco Jackson’s right. They bounced the Bears coach up and down so violently that Johnson’s left index finger, pointed in the air in victory, looked like it might whack the light fixture attached to the ceiling of the visiting locker room at Ford Field.</p><p>The celebration raged Thursday, minutes after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ 39-35 win moved them into first place in the NFC North and gave Johnson his first-ever win against his old employer. It continued when Rome Odunze, who caught the game-winning touchdown with six seconds left, handed Johnson a game ball and the coach smacked his thigh for another “Stanky Legg.”</p><p>Just two years ago, the Bears almost mutinied in the same locker room. Matt Eberflus had stood helplessly on the sideline, refusing to take a timeout as Caleb Williams was forced to heave a pass to Odunze as the clock expired. Players grumbled in disbelief, stunned at yet another end-game gaffe. Cornerback Jaylon Johnson yelled. Eberflus’ bosses decided enough was enough, firing the head coach the next morning.</p><p>Thursday, Johnson exorcised the ghost of Eberflus. Poetically, he did it by mastering what his predecessor could not — the end of the game.</p><p>“We’re a long way from there,” Odunze said. “Those are all bad tastes you have in your mouth, memories, but … it’s about the present.”</p><p>The present is thrilling — because coach and quarterback were stoic.</p><p>“I credit them a lot for staying completely poised throughout the process,” Johnson said. “There’s really not a whole lot of chaos. In moments like that, it’s an easy thing to do, to start freaking out. But they understand, we have it under control. We know what we’re doing from a coaching side. And for them, they’ve just gotta go out and play fast and execute the play-call.”</p><p>The old coach left Williams to stand helplessly on the field, watching the clock tick down. The new coach guided him to the end zone.</p><p>“I think you always revert back to your training,” Williams said. “You revert back to practice, you revert back to the conversations, you revert back to the moments that show up in practice. And we've had plenty of moments.”</p><p>The Bears’ final offensive possession was a master class in play-calling. It produced a touchdown, yes, but it bled all but three seconds off the clock. Johnson took his time.</p><p>“He was awesome,” Williams said.</p><p>It was a delicate situation to navigate, Johnson said.</p><p>“You wanted the touchdown, or at minimum to tie it up with a field goal,” he said, “but at the same time don’t want to give them any time left to respond.”</p><p>The Bears faced fourth-and-a-foot with two minutes to play when Johnson put running back Kyle Monangai at fullback and receiver Luther Burden at tailback — and had Williams run a sweep behind right tackle Darnell Wright for a first down. It was a play the team installed in a quarterback meeting Wednesday night.</p><p>About a minute later, the Bears faced third-and-five from the Lions’ 26 — and Johnson called another running play. Out of the shotgun, Williams pitched the ball left to D’Andre Swift, who ran for a first down. Swift’s 12-yard catch on the next play and a three-yard run on the one after that prompted Johnson to call the team’s last timeout with 13 seconds to play.</p><p>He had the Lions exactly where he wanted them. The Bears were at the 6, ready to take two shots into the end zone. If they failed, they’d kick a field goal to force overtime.</p><p>The first throw into the end zone was broken up. The second landed in Odunze’s arms as his toe tapped in the back right corner. The Bears, who hadn’t trailed in five full games before Thursday, took the lead for the first time Thursday with three seconds to play.</p><p>It was a beautiful plan, executed perfectly. Johnson trusted Williams not to take a sack on the final two throws — and the quarterback rewarded him.</p><p>“I think when he came here, people weren’t sure — obviously they knew the offensive pedigree — but if he could do it as a head coach,” left tackle Theo Benedet said. “It just keeps showing that he’s the best in the business to manage that.”</p><p>Johnson outcoached his mentor, Dan Campbell, whose failed decision to go for it on fourth-and-four from the Bears’ 33 with 2:22 to play — instead of kicking a field goal to go up six <br>— gave the Bears their final jolt of momentum. Jahmyr Gibbs, who had 205 rushing yards and 47 receiving yards, couldn’t shake linebacker T.J. Edwards.</p><p>Campbell made a controversial decision in the second quarter that ultimately paid off. On third-and-11 from their own 9 with 1:26 to play, Williams dropped back and fumbled the ball into the end zone. Right tackle Darnell Wright batted it forward to the Bears’ 10, where safety Brian Branch recovered it and lost four yards.</p><p>Wright was flagged for an illegal bat, which presented Campbell with two choices: to take a two-point safety and the ball after a free kick or no points and the ball at the 14.<br>He chose the former — and was rewarded when the Lions marched and scored on an 11-yard Sam LaPorta catch with 6 seconds to plays. The Lions went into the locker room up 19-10.</p><p>“I believed that we could get nine out of it instead of seven,” he said.</p><p>The Lions would need every single point. And even then, it wasn’t enough.</p><p>The game was personal for both sides. When receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown, one of Johnson’s favorite former players, made a one-handed catch in the first quarter, he celebrated with a “Stanky Legg,” a good-natured taunt toward his old coordinator.</p><p>Beating the Lions mattered to Johnson, too, even if he said later he was still processing it.</p><p>“He got his get-back,” Odunze said.</p>

entries.title: 'Tis the season, or at least the official start of the NFL season
entries.summary: <p>It’s a belief that Bill Belichick has carried with him and used as fuel for his players: “Football season doesn’t start until after Thanksgiving.”</p><p>Tom Brady uses that framework of thought to impart some understanding of the urgency switch that’s necessary when it comes to getting seven rings slid on your fingers.</p><p>Thanksgiving (which now includes Thanksgiving eve and Black Friday because of the NFL’s craving for societal takeover through sports) is not when the football season begins, though.</p><p>It is when the football season undeniably becomes official.</p><p>All playoff contenders take shape and position. All schemes and outcomes fall into play and place. It’s all derived from the 10-1 Lions vs. 11-0 Bears Thanksgiving game Nov. 29, 1934 (although not the first but the biggest at that time), that set the table (get it?) for the current iteration of this week’s “the rest of the season begins now” games the NFL masterfully scheduled.</p><p>How serious is the Thanksgiving threshold? Take the understandable benching/inactivation/release/falloff and fallout of future first ballot Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers by the Steelers going into Friday’s game. (For Mason Rudolph?) At 6-4 and tied for second at the time in the AFC North before Thanksgiving, every game meant something to the Steelers. After Thanksgiving, it’s down to every down having meaning.</p><p>The Week 12 NFL equator — from lukewarm to hot. Watch the level of productivity level up, physically, strategically and emotionally, from Thursday on by the Panthers, Browns, Giants, Rams and Seahawks in defense of their title. The latter two still have to play each other twice. Pay attention to how most, if not all of them, look different from Nov. 26 than they did before.</p><p>The Chiefs-Bills “generational holiday” game and the carryover from it. The Lions’ loss of Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell haunts them more. The Bengals’ and Packers’ running game hurts them more. The Vikings’ offense costs them more. The Broncos’ top-heavy schedule from the first half of the season helps them more than any other team in either conference. The scope and amplitude of the Seahawks-49ers “generational Sunday” game and the outcome of it.</p><p>All said, for this particular late November gateway, for no other team in the NFL does this framed belief in the season’s starting line hit its target more so than the Bears. For sure, no other team takes on the accuracy of the Belichick/Brady sentiment than them. Beginning on Thanksgiving, of the seven remaining games left for the Bears, five are against teams ranked in the top eight of the NFL’s and ESPN’s power rankings. With one of the other two (the Packers, a team that already has handed the Bears their worst loss this season) ranked in the top 12.</p><p>The true fight for the seven playoff spots in each conference takes over every practice, every film study, every 60 minutes in pads. Only six teams left with bye weeks, and none of them (including the Cowboys) is in a position of respectable circumstance to occupy one of those seven spots. Peaking early dismissed in thought. Things get real real quick. The stanky leg can only get stankier from here on out.</p><p>Supreme games with teams fighting for supremacy. The magnification of mistakes made by players and coaching staffs being the difference between avoiding wild-card weekend or even making it to Week 19.</p><p>Unctuous narratives and storylines to build up teams and hype up fan bases who in very particular situations and conditions know that the lies they tell themselves and force one another to believe do not stand any chance, even on any of the remaining given Thursdays, Mondays or Sundays of turning true.</p><p>It’s when the trap games should no longer exist let alone be lost. Moral victories, dead. After Thanksgiving, no teams should lose games they aren’t supposed to. No excuses rationalized as reasons. After Thursday, tolerance for any DK Metcalf or J.K. Dobbins or Brandon Aiyuk will be less than zero. Kirk Cousins and J.J. McCarthy no longer are given any rope of patience due to the short amount of time they’ve been on their respective teams.</p><p>Of the marathon that is every football season, this time of the year represents Miles 18-22.</p><p>Psychological combat, the physiological resilience, the physical fatigue, the mental questioning and doubt, fear of losing, pacing strategies, detrimental habits all become “The Wall” that teams who legitimately know they can win the Super Bowl push and break through.</p><p>It is here where the finish line is obsessed over, 26.2 the grail, not just a goal.</p><p>At this point, being the best teams doesn’t matter. The “want it more” kicks in, the “whole purpose” of NFL football begins . . . and stays. Wins mean less than losses because one loss from now until the end of the season could be the end of a season. Simply stated: After Thanksgiving, the game of football is replaced by the meaning of football. When every thing means everything.</p>

entries.title: Planes and trains have become a pain
entries.summary: <p>In America we're unable to win with any mode of transportation. Our airlines are in total disarray because of multiple flight delays. That is no thanks to the Department of Government "Deficiency" <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/faa-firings-trump-doge-safety-airlines-27390c6a7aac58063652302df5a243d3" target="_blank" >making 400 cuts</a> to the Federal Aviation Administration.</p><p>Now Amtrak is having its own problems. A few days ago, I was supposed to ride back to Chicago from Memphis by sleeping car. The morning before, I found out that my late evening train for the next day was canceled. So I took a bus back. When I spoke with an Amtrak ticket agent by phone, I learned that Amtrak’s City of New Orleans overnight train was experiencing mechanical problems.</p><p>I don’t blame Amtrak because it was <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2025/03/19/amtrak-ceo-resigns-trump-cuts/" target="_blank" >pressured</a> by the Trump administration to <a class="Link" href="https://www.progressiverailroading.com/amtrak/news/Amtrak-lays-off-250-cuts-another-200-open-management-roles--74500" target="_blank" >lay off 250 people and cut 200 </a>open management roles. With a limited number of employees Amtrak can only do so much. Thanks to Donald Trump and Elon Musk, our whole transportation system is dodgy. I’m happy that we have a new incoming Democratic Congress. At this point, that is all Americans can be happy about.</p><p><i>Shane Nodurft, Old Irving Park</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1f0000" name="module-1f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Be loyal, shop local</h3><p>Illinois families have an opportunity to make a meaningful difference in their communities this holiday season by supporting local businesses on Small Business Saturday this weekend.</p><p>Every day small-business owners work tirelessly to serve their customers, create jobs and strengthen their communities. From family-owned restaurants and retailers to manufacturers and service providers, these entrepreneurs are the backbone of Illinois' economy.</p><p>When you shop at a small business, your dollars stay local. They help support jobs, fuel local investment and sustain the businesses that sponsor youth sports teams, support charitable causes and help make our communities dynamic places to live and work.</p><p>Small businesses also offer something you won't find in a warehouse or on an app — personal service. The person helping you may be the owner who built the business from the ground up and is committed to earning your trust long after the holidays are over.</p><p>At a time when many small businesses continue to face rising costs, workforce challenges and an uncertain economic environment, your support matters more than ever. The<i> </i>National Federation of Independent Business<i> </i>is fighting for policies that lower the cost of doing business and reduce burdensome regulations, so Main Street businesses can continue to grow and create jobs.</p><p>But on Small Business Saturday, there's something everyone can do.</p><p>Shop local. Dine at a neighborhood restaurant. Purchase a gift card. Leave a positive review. Recommend your favorite small business to a friend.</p><p>These simple actions help strengthen local businesses and the communities that depend on them. This holiday season, let's support the Illinois entrepreneurs who invest in us every day.</p><p><i>Noah Finley, Illinois state director, National Federation of Independent Business </i></p><h3>Wrong way</h3><p>After President Donald Trump, a serial adulterer, declared Nvidia's Jensen Huang <a class="Link" href="https://www.the-independent.com/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-nvidia-call-jensen-huang-ceo-b3090058.html" target="_blank" >“did nothing wrong,”</a> I could only think of Joseph N. Welch’s response to Sen. Joseph McCarthy in 1954: <a class="Link" href="https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/june-9/joseph-mccarthy-meets-his-match" target="_blank" >“Have you no sense of decency, sir?”</a> </p><p>Putting aside whether Huang consorted with a Chinese spy, there’s no question he cheated on his wife. In my book and for most people, that’s doing something wrong.</p><p><i>Paul L. Newman, Merion Station, Pennsylvania</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Neighbor sees no difference between pets and livestock
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My neighbor's wife passed away recently. She had a cat, which she adored, but he is not a cat person. Shortly after his wife's death, he rigged up a contraption to his car exhaust pipe and killed the cat with carbon monoxide poisoning.</p><p>When I confronted him, he said it is legal for him to butcher a cow, decapitate a chicken, put a live lobster in a pot of boiling water and set out rat poison, so how is killing a cat any different as long as the method is humane? I don't really have a good answer for that. What do you think? — <i>FREAKED OUT IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR FREAKED OUT:</b> I am appalled at what your neighbor did. He's a monster. I'm sure a cat rescue group would have been happy to rehome that poor creature. What I think is that you should contact the Humane Society and ask someone there the question you just asked me. I believe what he did qualifies as animal cruelty.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a man in my 70s. I live alone, which I like. I'm thinking of moving closer to my grown child and their spouse and children. I'd like to watch the grandkids grow up (they are now in elementary school), and I get along well with their parents. The problem: I like the state and area I live in better than I'd enjoy living in their state. The parents and kids like where they live. That's where their jobs are and where they'll stay.</p><p>My health is generally pretty good, and I would not want to move in with them. They have their own lives and friends, and I can afford to live on my own. My close friend thinks I'd be miserable there. Another friend thinks I should move there to be close to family because I have no family here. One obvious answer is to ask "the kids" what they think, but I don't want to put them on the spot. What are they going to say, "No, we don't want you to move here"? Of course not. Any advice? — <i>UNDECIDED AT HOME</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNDECIDED:</b> I think you should ask them, but even if you could trust the kids' response to be completely honest, this is something you must decide for yourself. Do you agree that you'd be miserable there? Bear in mind that you would not be able to spend all your time with the grandkids. Do some research to see what local activities and attractions you might enjoy on your own. If you can't find anything that piques your interest, it might be best to stay put.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Is it rude for a visitor to your home to order food delivered for themselves and their partner? — <i>HUNGRY IN THE SOUTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR HUNGRY:</b> If your guests ordered food to be delivered to your home and did not include you, then it was rude. If you offered them something you prepared and they told you they preferred takeout, it was also rude. If I were you, and my feelings were hurt, I'd think twice about inviting them over again.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Time to give Sister a break, take care of older adults seriously
entries.summary: <p>Weaponized incompetence, misogyny and a broken healthcare system collided into a hilarious skit that the country can’t stop talking about.</p><p>By now, you’ve likely seen or heard about the “Saturday Night Live” satirical commercial <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbc.com/nbc-insider/snl-sister-sketch-caregivers-jane-wickline-john-mulaney" target="_blank" ><u>“Sister.” </u></a><u> </u>John Mulaney narrates that his dad means the world to him. But when he noticed him start to slow down, he needed to get the best care possible. A nursing home was off the table, and a private health aide cost too much.</p><p>“I didn't know where to turn. That's when I heard about sister,” Mulaney’s character says. “Sister is a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister. Now I don't have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”</p><p>Signing up for Sister is easy — no applications or insurance forms. She is the elder care system.</p><p>“Simply text 'dad fell' to sister, and she will quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country to take care of him.” </p><p>Men in the darkly funny commercial are gleeful and irresponsible. The viral skit speaks to women relating to the burden of solo caregiving and emotional toll of elder care. To say it struck a chord is an underestimation; the skit captured 1.2 million views less than 24 hours after airing on NBC.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a00000" name="module-a00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>“I've never had so many people send me a piece of content in my entire life. It was really remarkable,” said <a class="Link" href="https://www.aspenideas.org/speakers/ai-jen-poo?utm_source=google&utm_medium=adgrant&utm_campaign=&utm_term=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23372341321&gbraid=0AAAAADi6Fin1obkYYG6AE7zqJEzVELUX0&gclid=Cj0KCQiAiJXYBhD_ARIsAAx2AHm3FgDa1mPcon1PPSsnPLJeoV3IQizH4MtdJkyqAf4Ri_ZRLuQ83Q4aAj6QEALw_wcB" target="_blank" >Ai-jen Poo</a>, president of the National Domestic Workers Alliance. “We've never invested in the kind of policies or systems or workforce to support these essential universal human needs. We've just expected that women will shoulder it, or someone in the family will make big sacrifice. That's not sustainable given the demographic reality that we're living where every day 11,400 of us turn 65 and 10,000 babies are born.”</p><p>Poo, who is based in the Chicago area, said the median income for home care workers is $23,000 per year, and unpaid caregiving (like Sister) is valued at $648 billion a year. Personal care aides and certified nursing assistants are among the fastest growing jobs, yet they are supplementing their income with side gigs such as rideshare driving or donating plasma.</p><p>This is a policy choice. And it doesn’t have to be.</p><p>A first step is to invest in Medicaid, Poo said, where 70% of home care workers work through the program. Increased funding for Medicaid home and community-based services would expand access and raise wages.</p><p>“Right now, there are about 600,000 people on a waiting list who are actually eligible for the services but can't get access because there isn't enough funding there,” Poo said. A Democratic-sponsored bill in Congress called the <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8541" target="_blank" ><u>Long-Term Care Workforce Act</u></a> “would totally modernize the workforce and treat the workforce like the professional, dignified workforce that it is.”</p><p>Our most vexing social issues aren’t intractable. Solutions abound. But political will stalls. Helping our most vulnerable members of society isn’t a priority. Throw in how the caregiving labor is feminized, and you really have a low priority. Poo said change is coming. After the blue tsunami during this month’s midterm election, she said the new Congress has a mandate from voters about affordability. Another obvious policy choice is to expand Medicare coverage for long-term care and open it up to everyone, regardless of age.</p><p>Imagine a fully funded healthcare system where elders can age in place. Imagine caregivers earning respectable wages. Imagine Sister unburdened. She could enjoy time on a speedboat like her wayward brother does in the SNL skit. It’s a scenario in which elders are properly cared for — a kind of freedom not enough families experience.</p><p><i>Natalie Y. Moore is a senior lecturer at Northwestern University. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f70000" name="module-f70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 10 classical, jazz and world music concerts in Chicago to watch this holiday season
entries.summary: <p>Time to unpack the box of holiday shows! Oh, look, there’s that Messiah you love, a little dusty, maybe, but we can spruce it up with a new soloist. And there’s a choir concert with a grab bag of carol arrangements, which will do the job if we can replace a few bulbs.</p><p>But let me show you what I found in this other box — there are several things in here that come out only once every few years, or are surprising and different takes on holiday themes or are fixtures that decorate the holiday calendar dependably every year but have a shiny new bauble sparkling on them.</p><p>Everything here has something special in it, at least one fleeting element that’s unique to this December. of Chicago. The composer, Mario Castelnuovo-Tedesco, sprinkled in quotations from classical music and opera throughout the show as inside jokes for music buffs, showing off the composer’s wit to complement Wilde’s in the play. Castelnuovo-Tedesco scored the opera for two pianos and percussion, a stripped-down orchestration that suits Chicago Opera Theater’s streamlined style. This production marks the opera’s Chicago premiere.<br><i>Studebaker Theater, 410 S. year, lovers of the all-male chamber-choir sound have a second option for the holiday season to go with Chanticleer’s annual visit: the Minnesota-based octet Cantus, who have visited the Chicago area in the past, but have never before performed at as high-profile a venue as Ravinia. Cantus’ holiday program takes the format of a lessons and carols service, where the carols are a mixture of arrangements of well-known holiday music and contemporary compositions, and the lessons are bespoke poetry by Michael Kleber-Diggs. And it doesn’t conflict with Chanticleer on Dec. 8, so you could make it to both.<br><i>Ravinia, 201 Ravinia Park Rd., Highland Park. $46-$56. </i><a class="Link" href="http://ravinia.org/" target="_blank" ><i><u>ravinia.org</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 3-12: Riccardo Muti</h3><p>If you’re about to skip this item, thinking, “Ho-hum, Riccardo Muti, that guy’s here all the time,” turn that sleigh right around. Since the Chicago Symphony Orchestra beatified him as “music director emeritus for life” and he stepped away from the music directorship, his appearances have become rarer. <b>Muti leads one program on Dec. 3-5 with Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8 and the oboe concerto of Richard Strauss. </b>On Dec. 10-12, he follows that up with Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 24 with Yefim Bronfman and waltzes by other Strausses of the non-Richard, waltzier sort, fare that is more typical of New Year’s celebrations, but if you squint you can see 2027 up ahead somewhere.<b> </b>After this stint, the only Muti currently on the CSO’s schedule is an all-Rossini program in April.<br><i>Chicago Symphony Center, 220 S. Michigan Ave. $45+ for the Dec. 3-5 performances and $49 for the Dec. 10-12 concerts. </i><a class="Link" href="http://chicagosymphony.org/" target="_blank" ><i><u>chicagosymphony.org</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 5: poor hymnal</h3><p>The postminimalist composer David Lang is an interesting figure. For him, there’s a lot living in the “post-” of that term, as his music eschews the robotic, numbing qualities of minimalism to find a powerful emotional core in its repetitive sounds. In his three-year-old concert-length work “poor hymnal,” he imagines the shared songs of a religion stripped of everything except the exhortation for compassion, stringing together texts collected from not only religious writings but also political sources and scraped from online. The William Ferris Chorale, Chicago’s foremost choir of new music, has chosen “poor hymnal” as its holiday concert, a bold choice for a choir’s most prominent moment on the calendar.<br><i>Church of the Atonement, 5749 N. Kenmore Ave. $15-$40. </i><a class="Link" href="http://williamferrischorale.org/" target="_blank" ><i><u>williamferrischorale.org</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 5: Bria Skonberg</h3><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The jazz trumpeter and singer Bria Skonberg traces her musical lineage to Louis Armstrong, a fellow member of the flock of rare jazzbirds with vocal facility to rival that on their instruments. But while Satchmo’s vocal charm was like a rough but warming shot of hooch, Skonberg’s singing is a smooth bourbon that needs no chaser. Or maybe the rum in the eggnog, as she plays a show titled Jingle Bell Swing, likely covering some of her 2025 EP “Christmas Is” and her standalone cover of “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” which some would say makes the case for the song as a newly minted Christmas classic better than Mariah Carey does.<br><i>Winter’s Jazz Club, 465 N. McClurg Ct. $38-$48. </i><a class="Link" href="http://wintersjazzclub.com/" target="_blank" ><i><u>wintersjazzclub.com</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 13: Wayang</h3><p>Gamelan music, traditional to Indonesia, unspools from an ensemble of mostly percussion instruments, all playing together like an orchestra. Mallet instruments, drums, gongs and other sounds in non-Western tuning systems can give the music a hypnotic quality that some listeners fall in love with. The local organization Friends of the Gamelan, nicknamed FROG, this year presents a traditional Javanese shadow-puppet show with gamelan accompaniment, something they haven’t done in 20 years. In Java, a wayang kulit show can last eight hours, but here FROG limits itself to four, and sets it up so you can jump in and out as you please.<br><i>Epiphany Center for the Arts, 201 S. Ashland Ave. Free.</i><a class="Link" href="http://epiphanychi.com" target="_blank" ><i><u>epiphanychi.com</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 16: Concert for Peace</h3><p>Stephen Burns, the founder and artistic director of Fulcrum Point New Music Project, has a personal connection to several of the world’s major religions. He said one thing they can all agree on is peace. For 28 years, Burns has marshaled the forces and friends of his world-music-tinged ensemble to put on a concert promoting pacific principles, often around the winter holidays. This year’s program features two musicians whose omnivorous styles encompass not only classical-tradition propriety but also rap, pop and electronica: Gene Pritsker and the Dutch composer whose <i>nom de guerre</i> — here let’s call it a <i>nom de paix</i> — is JacobTV.<br><i>Fourth Presbyterian Church of Chicago, 126 E. so they come again for Messiahs. Many musical organizations, counting on hallelujah-mad audiences, program it as dependably as the fall turns to winter — but you know who doesn’t? The Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So the twice or three times a decade when the CSO and its chorus do perform it, it’s a happening. This time around, the CSO’s Messiah will present two notable local debuts: the Japanese baroque specialist Masaaki Suzuki conducting, and the countertenor Hugh Cutting singing the alto solos.<br><i>Chicago Symphony Center, 220 S. Michigan Ave. $69+.</i><a class="Link" href="http://chicagosymphony.org/" target="_blank" ><i><u>chicagosymphony.org</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 18-19: Matt Wilson’s Christmas Tree-O</h3><p>Kitsch and Christmas string together like cranberries and popcorn, a partnership that can revel in the predictability of the holiday. (Note to self: “Kitschmas” as an album title.) The drummer Matt Wilson has for years been camping up holiday music sacred and secular with his seasonal Christmas Tree-O, alongside a bass, a saxophone and a buzz of cheery jesting. Despite the lighthearted treatments, the jazz is still seriously high quality, with a full harmonic texture even without a piano or guitar playing chords. It’s easy to shade cynical around the holidays, so every once in a while it’s good to have a reminder that cheese is delicious.<br><i>Green Mill, 4802 N. entries.title: Chicago's TIF program to help blighted neighborhoods has fallen short on the West Side
entries.summary: <p>Sears, Roebuck and Co. once employed thousands of workers at a 40-acre plant on the West Side where it produced the thick mail-order catalogs sent to homes across America.</p><p>Today, the former Sears facility looms over vacant lots and boarded-up churches, the hollowed-out skyline of a neighborhood that has been waiting for a comeback promised long ago by city officials.</p><p>About five miles east, in Downtown Chicago, a city tax-diversion program intended to revitalize blighted neighborhoods has helped stimulate employment and fund the development of gleaming skyscrapers, luxury housing and parks.</p><p>But on the West Side, where decades of underinvestment and rising costs have contributed to entrenched poverty, it has largely failed, The New York Times has found. That's in part because of shifting political priorities and fractured oversight by city agencies of the tax-increment financing program, or TIF.</p><p>The disparity has long been apparent to people who live on the West Side, where many say their neighborhoods have been neglected for years and that grocery stores, new schools and job opportunities remain scarce.</p><p>The TIF program is under debate as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/mayor-brandon-johnson" >Mayor Brandon Johnson </a>says he is trying to prioritize funding for low-income neighborhoods.</p><div by a bond program that can use expired TIF funds.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joshua Lott | The New York Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A spokesman for the mayor said the city would keep working to “advance a more equitable vision for economic development, one that breaks from decades of uneven investment and puts public resources to work in the communities that need them most.”</p><p>The program is intended to jump-start public and private development in struggling areas. After the city draws a TIF district, tax revenue from rising property values within its borders is set aside to be reinvested in the area.</p><p>The Times compared projects in three of the poorest neighborhoods on the West Side — North <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lawndale" >Lawndale,</a> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/east-garfield-park" >East Garfield Park</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/west-garfield-park" >West Garfield Park</a> — to those in three similarly sized Downtown neighborhoods.</p><p>Over the past three decades, the TIF districts that included those downtown neighborhoods collected nearly $5 billion in revenue, more than double the $2 billion collected by the West Side districts.</p><p>Downtown, over $1 billion has been spent on projects, including affordable housing, a top program priority. Just over $100 million has been spent on such projects in the West Side neighborhoods.</p><p>Our examination focused on 16 housing developments in the three West Side neighborhoods.</p><p>One TIF redevelopment plan there projected increases in property values assuming the renovation of 1,000 residential units by 2036. The plan, created in 2000, was amended in 2015 to enlarge the project and extend its deadline.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-710000" name="image-710000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27235a7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1266x711+0+66/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F01%2F095e209f4b47ae0268f8b9bc60ad%2Fthe-success-of-the-tif-program-in-downtown-chicago-never-fully-reached-the-west-side-credit-joshua-lott-for-the-new-york-times.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9947cc7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1266x711+0+66/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F01%2F095e209f4b47ae0268f8b9bc60ad%2Fthe-success-of-the-tif-program-in-downtown-chicago-never-fully-reached-the-west-side-credit-joshua-lott-for-the-new-york-times.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a61062/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1266x711+0+66/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd2%2F01%2F095e209f4b47ae0268f8b9bc60ad%2Fthe-success-of-the-tif-program-in-downtown-chicago-never-fully-reached-the-west-side-credit-joshua-lott-for-the-new-york-times.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A building on the West Side. </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Collapsed floors, little oversight</h3><p>Chicago has used TIF more extensively than any other major American city, building it into a $16.6 billion initiative, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/26/tif-tax-increment-financing-property-taxes-chicago-uic-great-cities-institute" target="_blank" ><u>recent study by the Great Cities Institute,</u></a> an economic research hub at the University of Illinois Chicago.</p><p>The program was an attempt to give a boost to troubled neighborhoods and address economic and racial disparities while developing city centers and attracting private investment.</p><p>It began in Chicago in 1984 under Mayor Harold Washington as a way to offset a decline in federal funding for urban development. Initially, it saw money being spent downtown, but Washington insisted that investment also reach the West Side. Daley applied the program more broadly, including tapping it for wealthier neighborhoods.</p><p>TIF money typically provides a small but integral slice of a project's funding. Paired with city, state or federal dollars, it pays for infrastructure and debt payments. It also can go toward private development, like skyscrapers, covering site-preparation costs including demolition and facade work. For affordable and mixed-income housing, TIF dollars can fund construction. Developers generally aren't handed money upfront but are reimbursed later on with TIF revenue.</p><p>Chicago’s mayors have pushed reforms aimed at spending more in underinvested areas, but critics say TIF has focused too heavily on Downtown and diverted revenue needed for public services citywide.</p><p>Supporters say TIF transformed Chicago into a global city, generating investment and jobs.</p><p>“Everybody wants to talk about the failings of how TIF didn’t live up to its promise,” said Gery Chico, a former chief of staff to Daley. “What would have happened to those areas if TIF didn’t exist?”</p><p>By the 1990s, Sears, Sunbeam and other employers had left the West Side, erasing many blue-collar jobs and, with those, incentive for investment. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Deborah Mitchell says that, for years, she has regularly called the property manager of her building, Lawndale Apartments, to complain about her unit.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joshua Lott | The New York Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Deborah Mitchell, a caretaker for her disabled niece, said she has regularly complained to the property manager of Lawndale Apartments about her unit, which costs her about $900 a month on top of a federal housing subsidy.</p><p>Mitchell, 66, said the floor was warped, the bedroom doors wouldn’t shut, and mice droppings coated the kitchen shelves. Common areas are no better: Tenants dispose of cooking grease on staircases, she said. Garbage, old bed frames and broken refrigerators litter a vacant lot next door.</p><p>Peter Holsten, president of the development company that owns the building, said his staff tried to respond promptly to life-threatening concerns, but, with high staff turnover, some repairs were not made.</p><p>When he acquired 170 units in the aging buildings in 2006 from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, he agreed to keep apartments subsidized and to renovate them, using $8.9 million in TIF funds. He addressed numerous safety and health violations, records show, but said he couldn’t afford to fix everything. Instead of replacing water-damaged floors, he said, workers covered them with plywood and carpet. By 2009, the number of violations had declined.</p><p>The next year, though, the short-term solutions had started to fail, inspection records show, and violations began racking up. In 2023, after tenant complaints landed him in court, Holsten applied for $10 million in TIF funds for improvements. His application, like most, was not chosen.</p><p>Former city officials and affordable housing developers said rehab projects were often costlier than anticipated, and, unlike new construction, they displaced residents.</p><p>Earlier this year, construction began on a 107-unit rehab project, in part with $10 million in TIF funds. It is the first such effort in the three West Side neighborhoods in about a decade.</p><p>Records from many of the other 16 housing projects on the West Side document deferred maintenance: crumbling porches, cracking walls, building fires and vacancies.</p><p>Liberty Square Apartments in East Garfield Park, for example, received a TIF commitment for hundreds of thousands of dollars, along with other funding, in 2004 for 12 new buildings. But, in 2017, the apartments failed a state inspection. Six years later, about one-third of the units were vacant, records show. A new owner is now repairing and leasing units, according to city officials.</p><h3>Some struggle to get funding</h3><p>Developers said they have struggled to get TIF funding or political support from their aldermen, whose approval the city requires before greenlighting projects. In interviews, a dozen developers described a bottleneck: It isn't just money, they say; it is whom you know.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> them moved to the West Side, where city officials promised development. TIF funded community centers, a hospital renovation, a small-business hub, a theater and a garden in the three West Side neighborhoods examined for this report. Some say it’s not enough.</p><p>“The schools and the clinics are bad,” said Shanique George, 34, a mother of five and housekeeper who lives in East Garfield Park. “They don’t care about us.”</p><p>George said her apartment, partly funded through TIF, is “decent.” But she remembers the services she grew up with in Cabrini-Green, where she attended ballet classes through her church and lived near a library and grocery store. Now, the only large grocery store within a mile of her home — a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" target="_blank" ><u>Save A Lot</u></a> that received $2 million in TIF funds — closed in July.</p><p>Cheatham, the father who worries about his children’s safety, said he was surprised his housing application had been chosen. He said he has bad credit and had served time for a drug-dealing conviction.</p><p>Affordable rents for subsidized<b> </b>housing are calculated from the area's median income, including affluent suburbs. Cheatham says his $1,500 monthly rent is out of reach for many North Lawndale residents like him: a Black man, raised in public housing, with a factory job.</p><p>Almost a year after moving in, he said, he's just one missed paycheck away from falling behind.</p><p>“Even though it’s home, it’s not viable,” he said.</p><p>Tenants at four other mixed-income developments in the West Side neighborhoods, built in part with TIF dollars, described similar strain.</p><p>In Chicago, TIF districts last 23 years, with the option to extend to 35. When dozens of TIF districts expire over the next 15 years, an estimated $2.2 billion is expected to return to Chicago’s general fund, according to a city planning document.</p><p>Some will go toward a new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/03/12/mayor-brandon-johnson-1-25-billion-borrowing-plan-housing-economic-development-city-council-oversight" >bond program, approved by the Johnson administration in 2024, </a>which aims to invest up to $1.25 billion in housing and real estate development by 2028. The administration says the program, which allows spending outside TIF districts, will prioritize affordable housing and projects on the South Side and the West Side — though some say it should go toward other city services.</p><p>Ald. Monique Scott (24th), whose ward includes North Lawndale and parts of East Garfield Park and West Garfield Park, joined the mayor at a ribbon-cutting last month for a housing project subsidized by the bond program. The lot, she said, had been vacant since she was a little girl.</p><p>Still, Scott said, other developers in her ward told her they had trouble accessing bond funding.</p><p>“TIF is important, and it can help move a community forward,” she said. “But people just give up.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Justin Mayo, Sheelagh McNeill </i></p><p><i>This article was reported in partnership with Big Local News at Stanford University. entries.title: More PPP fraud: Illinois prison chaplain took COVID-19 relief cash in bogus business scheme, watchdog finds
entries.summary: <p>An Illinois prison chaplain pocketed thousands of dollars in federal COVID-19 relief money in a scam orchestrated by an assistant prison warden who collected kickbacks for arranging bogus loans for corrections employees through the federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ppp-paycheck-protection-program-covid-relief" target="_blank" >Paycheck Protection Program,</a> state investigators found.</p><p>The Rev. Damien Davis' case is striking not only because of his former position as a spiritual and moral adviser to prison inmates but also because it illustrates how workplace relationships helped fuel pandemic-relief fraud among Illinois government employees.</p><p>In a new report, Susan Haling, the state of Illinois's executive inspector general, says her office completed 589 investigations involving PPP loans through the end of June. Nearly three of every four of those investigations — 427 in all — resulted in findings of misconduct.</p><p>In some cases, including the one involving Davis, state employees enlisted the help of colleagues to obtain money under false pretenses from the federal program that was designed to help struggling businesses stay afloat during the coronavirus pandemic. The loans generally weren't required to be repaid as long as the recipients used the money for allowable expenses, like payroll and overhead.</p><p>To land his $20,832 loan from the program, Davis, 43, said on his application he had a security business with $100,000 in yearly sales, but the business didn't exist, according to records released by the inspector general's office.</p><p>The chaplain later admitted to investigators that he didn't own such a business, telling them he needed the money because he'd been a victim of identity theft.</p><p>Davis, who was a chaplain at Stateville Correctional Center near Joliet from 2017 to 2023, told investigators that an assistant warden arranged for an unidentified Chicago woman to fill out his loan application in 2020. The assistant warden got $2,000 from Davis. The woman got $5,000. And Davis used more than $13,000 of the money to pay off his credit-card bills, investigators said.</p><p>Most of the loan was later forgiven, meaning Davis didn't have to pay back the money.</p><p>The assistant warden also took kickbacks of $2,000 to $5,000 for arranging fraudulent loans for at least four other corrections employees whose names were blacked out of the inspector general's report.</p><p>The assistant warden was fired in 2023 and died in March, records show.</p><p>State investigative reports show more than 20 Illinois state corrections employees were found to have defrauded the federal loan program out of at least $580,000.</p><p>Unlike many government workers who worked from home during the pandemic, correctional officers continued to see one another regularly at the prisons where they worked — circumstances that law enforcement sources say appeared to make them more likely to have been drawn into PPP fraud networks.</p><p>Davis is among at least a dozen state corrections employees who have faced criminal charges in Cook County for defrauding the federal program. His case and others was prosecuted by the Illinois attorney general's office.</p><p>Davis and others have pleaded guilty to fraud charges and been sentenced to what's called "Second Chance" probation, which lets them avoid having a conviction on their records if they successfully complete their sentences. Davis agreed to repay the loan and finished his probation in July, court records show.</p><p>He resigned from his state job in late 2023, after the inspector general recommended he be fired.</p><p>According to Davis' social media postings, he has continued to work as a chaplain for a hospital and to lecture about a book he wrote. He and a lawyer who represented him couldn't be reached for comment.</p><p>In a written statement to investigators, Davis admitted that his loan application was bogus but said his “intentions were not malicious” and pleaded to keep his state job.</p><p>Davis also told investigators he hadn't given the woman who filled out his application the phony information about the supposed security business.</p><p>But investigators weren't swayed.</p><p>“Regardless of the ease of procuring these PPP funds, this was not free money for the taking,” they wrote. “State employees are expected, at minimum, to maintain the public's trust and confidence.”</p><p>Nationwide, pandemic-relief programs were plagued by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ppp-paycheck-protection-program-covid-relief/2026/10/15/ppp-fraud-chicago-police-department-paycheck-protection-program-david-glockner-covid-relief" target="_blank" >fraud on a staggering scale</a>.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times previously has reported that, in Chicago, people got loans from programs including PPP for purported farms with Downtown addresses, Cook County Jail inmates secured loans for nonexistent businesses and people living in homeless shelters obtained money meant to help struggling businesses stay afloat as the spread of the coronavirus shut them down and drained their finances.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li entries.summary: <p>Just because it’s the holidays doesn’t mean Chicago’s concert calendar is winding down any time soon. From the return of Wilco’s Winterlude to an indie-rock doubleheader of Interpol and Modest Mouse and a chance to catch Grammy darling Raye, we are counting down the top 10 shows to catch in December. After buying everyone else gifts, it’s time to treat yourself with some tickets, too.</p><h3>Dec. 1: Jim James</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-credit"><p>Danny Clinch</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The ringleader of My Morning Jacket released his first solo album in eight years in August and is now unpacking its delicate beauty during a short run of solo acoustic shows. Called “Wowed Out,” the record title comes from James’ own phrase for society’s battle with chronic overstimulation. To combat overwhelming anyone further, his new compositions, like the title track and “Come Again,” are soft and sparse explorations of existentialism and survival with a familiar palette of soul, psychedelia and roots music. All the songs are also achingly cinematic, which makes sense since most were originally intended for film scores before finding wider purpose. <i>Vic Theatre, 3145 N. Sheffield. $62.75+. </i><a class="Link" href="http://axs.com" target="_blank" ><i><u>axs.com</u></i></a></p><h3>Dec. 4-5 and 7-8: Wilco Winterlude</h3><p>Wilco is scratching the seven-year itch. For the first time since 2019, the beloved Chicago mainstays are reviving their year-end Winterlude series at home with two dates at Chicago Theatre, Dec. 4-5, and two dates at Thalia Hall, Dec. 7-8, a venue the full band has surprisingly never played. The special shows come ahead of international dates in Morocco, Portugal and Spain next year, so it’s the only chance to see the group around town (for now), and naturally it’s a tough ticket to nab. But if you are going, request songs for the set on the band’s official website. <i>Chicago Theatre (Dec. 4-5), 175 N. State St., and Thalia Hall (Dec. 7-8), 1807 S. Allport. Indie rocker Ben Kweller will lead the New Year’s countdown at SPACE with a set spanning his power-pop ballads, melodic alt-country and everything in between. This year, Kweller marks 20 years of his groundbreaking self-titled album in 2006 (in which he played every album himself) while also channeling grief into purpose on his latest album, “Cover the Mirrors” about the journey back after losing his teen son a few years ago. entries.title: Bears treating TE Colston Loveland as week-to-week
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are treating tight end Colston Loveland as week-to-week after he hurt his knee Thursday, a source said, though they are still conducting tests Friday.</p><p>That the team hasn't ruled out a return to action this season counts as a win, given the alternative.</p><p>Loveland was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-lions-colston-loveland-carted-to-locker-room-tight-end-thursday-ford-field" target="_blank" >shoved backward</a> by linebacker Trevor Nowaske and over running back D’Andre Swift at the end of a two-yard run in the first quarter Thursday. He went to the blue injury tent and then to the cart, where he covered his face with a towel. The Bears quickly ruled him out for the game, which is unusual for a team that typically calls players questionable.</p><p>The former first-round pick has 41 catches for 397 yards and three touchdowns this season. Earlier in the first quarter against the Lions, Loveland fumbled the ball away after a five-yard catch.</p><p>He has spent half the season without Cole Kmet. His fellow tight end tore his knee against the Patriots and had surgery to repair ligaments. He's out for the year.</p><p>The Bears' two remaining tight ends with NFL experience are rookie Sam Roush, who had five catches Thursday, and veteran Stephen Carlson, who made his first catch since 2019 against the Lions. </p><p>"I’ve got a lot of confidence in [Roush] as a blocker," Bears coach Ben Johnson said. "We saw him – we threw to him, I think he had five catches this game, and so he’s become the security blanket there for our quarterback as well. We’ll see if he needs to have a bigger role here going forward. And then Carlson ... He’s dependable, he does everything right, and we’re going to use him at some point. And here we go, in one of the biggest games that we’ve had in a year and a half, and he doesn’t miss a beat."</p>

entries.title: Over 200 ComEd workers trek to St. Louis to help restore power after winter storms
entries.summary: <p>Over 200 ComEd workers went to St. Louis after tens of thousands of residents were without power Thanksgiving morning from a severe winter storm. </p><p>The workers took off for St. Louis Thursday afternoon and are helping repair damage and restore service as "quickly and safely as possible" after completing safety training, according to ComEd. </p><p>On Thursday morning, about 123,000 households and businesses were without power, Ameren said in a statement. As of Friday morning, nearly 75,000 <a class="Link" href="https://outagemap.ameren.com/alerts/d25d6e6d-232b-4037-8a35-85753072cd2d" target="_blank" >Ameren</a> customers were still in the dark. </p><p>Ameren, which provides electricity to customers in both Illinois and Missouri, said it requested mutual aid and noted crews were working "around the clock to safely restore power with additional resources on the way." </p><p>The restoration effort is expected to take multiple days, according to Ameren. </p><p>This week is not the first time this year Ameren and ComEd have worked together. After tornadoes left over half a million customers in the Chicago area without power <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" >this past August</a>, Ameren sent workers to assist with restoration efforts. </p><p>"Ameren was very helpful for us this summer when we had big storms in the area," said John Schoen, a spokesperson with ComEd. "We were glad to be able to send some of our crews and some of our contractors out to help them."</p><p>ComEd is part of a string of mutual assistance networks around the country that sends workers and contractors to an area in need of extra staffing for restoration efforts at the expense of the requester. </p><p>Friday morning, 140 more crew members and contractors were sent to the East Coast to help some of the sister Exelon utilities that have been hit hard by storms. </p><p>"Whether it's here at home or whether it's doing mutual assistance like this, being able to bring the power back, especially during a holiday season, is the most impactful work they do," Schoen said. "They're out there trying to get people restored just as quickly and as safely as they can."</p>
