entries.title: Sky offseason position analysis: Ajsa Sivka stock rises but frontcourt still needs more defense
entries.summary: <p>Have the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> found their next Elena Delle Donne? The talking heads sure seem to think so. The Sky’s 21-year-old prospect, Ajsa Sivka, is drawing comparisons to the Hall of Famer as a freshman for the University of Kentucky.</p><p>Through six college games, Sivka (6'4) is showing off an enticing assortment of skills: she’s shooting 65% from downtown, including an 8-12 performance against NC State, and playmaking well for her teammates.</p><p>The Delle Donne comparisons <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2025/11/28/setting-expectations-for-20-year-old-sky-prospect-ajsa-sivka" >are a little outlandish</a>, but a moment in the national spotlight is well-deserved.</p><p>“I just laughed at all those little [preseason] watchlists — she’s not on any of them,” Kentucky coach Kenny Brooks said after the NC State game. “We just chuckled…She’s definitely one of the best players in the country. We knew that when we got her.”</p><p>For the Sky, the "Sivka Situation" is an odd one. Because the WNBA’s draft rules allow international prospects to be drafted earlier, the Sky selected her when she turned 19 in 2025. She already had professional experience under her belt in European leagues.</p><p>The Sky didn't expect her to join right away — Sivka prioritized her Slovenian national team commitments during the 2025 season — but they penciled her in as part of their young core and thought she would report for the 2026 season.</p><p>She ended up signing with Kentucky instead. Kids these days.</p><p>“I just wanted to be ready and feel confident once I go [to the WNBA],” Sivka said of her decision to play for Kentucky first.</p><p>Sivka will have a full four years of college eligibility at her disposal, and hasn’t yet indicated whether she’ll use them.</p><p>The Sky will be praying she's one and done — she's looking like a total steal as a late first-round draft pick. If she joined them in 2027, Sivka would immediately be their best shooter, and depending on how free agency shakes out, she’d have a shot at the starting rotation.</p><p>Not the kind of difference-maker you want doing keg stands in Kentucky for the next four years.</p><p><b>Frontcourt breakdown</b></p><p><b>WHO THE SKY HAVE:</b> Rickea Jackson, Kamilla Cardoso, Azura Stevens, Elizabeth Williams</p><p><b>WHO'S A FREE AGENT: </b>Aicha Coulibaly</p><p>One problem that Sivka will not solve is the Sky’s frontcourt defense. Her lanky frame means she’s better suited for guarding on the perimeter than banging down low.</p><p>The 2026 playoffs, however, were a sharp reminder that you can’t expect to go far without rim protection. The semifinal series between the Valkyries and the Aces basically posed the question: is it better to have A’ja Wilson, league’s best scorer, or a defensive center like Kiah Stokes? Believe it or not the answer this time around the answer was Stokes.</p><p>Her MVP-level impact throughout the playoffs draws into sharp relief the pickle that the Sky are in with building around Cardoso. Their 6’7 center has grown into a borderline All-Star because of her offense, but she still is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/09/29/sky-offseason-notebook-reviewing-kamilla-cardosos-development" >not a very good defender.</a></p><p>To address this, the Sky can either keep hoping she improves—she has the size and athleticism—or they can put significant pressure on whoever plays alongside her.</p><p>The Sky believe that their bouncy 25-year-old forward, Rickea Jackson, can help protect the rim once she returns from an ACL injury sometime next season. Like Cardoso, Jackson has the athletic tools to be a great defender, but also like Cardoso, is totally unproven. </p><p>There’s a risk to relying on these two.</p><p>The other issue in the frontcourt is veteran Azura Stevens. When they signed her to a 3-year, $3.1 million contract last offseason, they believed she was on the verge of breaking out into “superstar” territory. They also assumed she would help stretch the floor next to Cardoso.</p><p>But she ended up taking a step backward: her scoring, rebounding, and shot-blocking production all fell, and her 3-point percentage plummeted to 26%.</p><p>You can blame it on the halting nature of her season: she missed the first six games with a knee injury and then another four down the stretch for personal reasons. It's hard for anyone to find a rhythm that way.</p><p>That is, anyway, the story they should be selling potential trade partners. Dial up anyone who’s desperate for size and scoring, and can still visualize Stevens' 2025 campaign with the Sparks, when she shot 38% from deep.</p><p>If they can’t move her, and Sivka joins, the Sky will have a glut in the frontcourt, but no easy answers defensively.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Bulls brass has trade flexibility but will strike when time is right
entries.summary: <p>Bryson Graham gave away the answers to the test back in May when he was hired.</p><p>Seven months later, that hasn’t changed.</p><p>“Most rebuild situations is when you don’t have star-caliber players,” the executive vice president of basketball operations said then when discussing the roster and the immediate to-do list surrounding it. “Right now, not to say we don’t have anyone on this roster that can get there, but until we continue to draft well, add to this mix, and add overall talent and team identity, yeah, we’re in a rebuilding phase.”</p><p>Start with the “draft well …”</p><p>Caleb Wilson was a no-brainer at No. 4, the jury is still out on the development of No. 15 overall pick Dailyn Swain, while the two-way contract duo of Tobe Awaka and Jaylin Sellers have quietly been forcing their way into being rotation factors in the second half of the season.</p><p>The “team identity” part of the equation is an ongoing work in progress with first-year Bulls coach Tiago Splitter playing professor in that class. It’s now obvious what kind of team Splitter wants; playing up-tempo on offense and biting at arms and legs like dogs on defense.</p><p>When Splitter doesn’t see a player checking those boxes on both ends of the floor he uses playing time – or lack thereof – as a reminder.</p><p>Where it will get interesting for Graham and the rest of the front office is the “add to this mix … add overall talent” part of this. The trade rumors are already out there for the Bulls, courtesy of outsiders throwing whatever they can scoop up at a wall.</p><p>According to a Bulls source, there is absolutely nothing imminent on the trade front besides the usual fact-finding that goes on in late November. Because of the new 3-2-1 draft lottery system, even the bottom-feeder teams are still trying to jockey for standings position to stay out of the lower three, which means the usual trade flurry could stay stagnant until right before the Feb. 11 deadline this year.</p><p>The only team that might break ranks in that department is Sacramento, which has been a sinking ship since the season tipped off. While Domantas Sabonis and former Bull Zach LaVine haven’t officially made trade requests, it’s known league-wide that both are begging for a change of address.</p><p>According to an NBA source, LaVine is as unhappy as he’s ever been in a situation but is still trying to keep the locker room afloat. The guard is in the last year of his max contract, making just under $49 million this season, and is hoping to land on a playoff roster, coming off the bench if needed.</p><p>As far as the Bulls and the rumors that have popped up around them? Meaningless static.</p><p>Of course, there are no untouchables currently on the roster besides the rookie wearing No. 8. Graham all but made that clear Day 1 on the job. The likes of Norman Powell and Zach Collins were signed to two-year deals, with Year 2 being a team option, for a reason.</p><p>He built this roster to be able to stay very fluid. Fluid come late January and into the deadline, however.</p><p>Right now, the goal is to continue building a play-style identity, while developing all the young talent. Signs that Splitter has been doing just that courtesy of a 5-3 record over the last eight games after a dismal 1-9 start to the 2026-27 campaign. To do that, however, pieces need to stay in place for now.</p><p>Graham will make sure they do.</p><p>So Josh Giddey being linked to the Suns or a Jalen Smith heading to Philadelphia? Fun late-November chatter that falls under the category of unsubstantiated blather.</p><p>How so? The answers to the test were given months ago.</p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkulykt-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Sun-Times staff</a></h5><p>Under cloudy skies, this year's Thanksgiving parade started an hour earlier, thanks to the Bears broadcast, stepping off around 7:45 a.m. as hundreds lined State Street to watch.</p><p>The procession, the city's 92nd, marched toward Randolph Street and featured 14 balloon floats, 12 marching bands and performances from numerous local cultural groups, and of course, the Jesse White Tumblers. This year's parade also introduced a new Cookie Monster balloon.</p><p>Charles "Peanut" Tillman, a Bears cornerback for 12 seasons, was the parade's grand marshal. Actor Jake Connelly, of "Stranger Things" fame, waved from a Mercedes convertible, just in front of the Nutcracker balloon float.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkulykt-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>MORE PHOTOS HERE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Beyond just reheating, what's your tip for re-serving Thanksgiving leftovers?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Grammy nominee Lil’ Ed Williams is carrying the Chicago blues tradition forward
entries.summary: <p>When the 2027 Grammy nominations were announced earlier this month, several <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/11/16/2027-grammy-awards-list-chicago-raye-rosalia-mavis-staples-ye-j-ivy" target="_blank" ><u>Chicagoans were on the list</u></a>. But perhaps most underrated is local blues artist Lil’ Ed Williams, who earned his first Grammy nod at age 71.</p><p>Williams’ sound is pure Blues.  It's all slide guitar and raw emotion. Hutto. Hutto won a Grammy for Best Traditional Blues Recording in 1985.</p><p>Now, Williams has a Grammy nomination of his own.</p><p>He and his band, the Blues Imperials, are up for<a class="Link" href="https://www.grammy.com/awards/categories/best-traditional-blues-album/" target="_blank" ><u> Best Traditional Blues Album</u></a> for their latest release, “Slideways.” Williams’ particular gift is the slide guitar, that high-energy, bold sound that emulates artists like Hound Dog Taylor.</p><p>That classic blues style is what Iglauer has liked about Williams’ music from day one. And I said, in the one of the most fateful phrases that I've ever used, ‘Would you like to do a few more?’ By the end of the evening we had cut 30 songs and we had a debut album.”</p><p>Forty years and 10 albums later, Williams has his first Grammy recognition.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

entries.title: Where will Bears QB Caleb Williams look now that top TEs Cole Kmet, Colston Loveland are injured?
entries.summary: <p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> think of tight end Cole Kmet, the first image is him making an over-the-shoulder catch in the snow on quarterback Caleb Williams’ jaw-dropping heave against the Rams in the playoffs last season.</p><p>With fellow tight end Colston Loveland, perhaps it would be him hurdling a Saints defender on his way to a touchdown a week ago.</p><p>Both of those weapons are off the table now.</p><p>With Kmet out for the season and Loveland suffering a significant knee injury in the Thanksgiving win over the Lions, Williams will have to look elsewhere. The team’s early impression of Loveland’s injury is that he could return this season, but it’s unlikely to be soon.</p><p>In a literal sense, rookie Sam Roush and journeyman Stephen Carlson are suddenly their top two tight ends, but on a practical level, it surely means Williams will be relying even more heavily on wide receivers Rome Odunze and Luther Burden and running back D’Andre Swift.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson spent the offseason dreaming up plans for Kmet, Loveland and Roush, so the injuries have severely undercut him. However, as he worked with general manager Ryan Poles on personnel decisions, his goal was to fortify the offense to such an extent that it could survive losing some pieces.</p><p>Considering Johnson has been patching it together at left tackle throughout his first two seasons, he’ll probably find a solution for this problem as well.</p><p>All eyes are on Odunze, as they absolutely should be. He was the No. 9 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, coming in with Williams, and teams expect those players to develop into All-Pros. To date, he’s been good, not great.</p><p>He’s trending upwardly, though. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-draft-dream-comes-true-as-qb-caleb-williams-wr-rome-odunze-lead-39-35-win-over-lions" >Not only did Odunze catch the winning touchdown pass from Williams with three seconds left to beat the Lions</a>, but he has 18 catches for 279 yards and three touchdowns over his last four games and put himself on pace for his first 1,000-yard season.</p><p>The Bears will need more from Burden, too, which will be music to his ears after just five catches over the last two games. He’s certainly capable of high production: Over the four games before that, he caught 26 passes for 378 yards three touchdowns.</p><p>Johnson also pivoted to making Swift a bigger part of the passing attack after Loveland went down Thursday, and he racked up a career-high 97 yards receiving on seven catches. It was a callback to their 2021 and ’22 seasons together in Detroit, when Swift got a total of 148 targets.</p><p>Williams, by the way, managed without Loveland for most of the game Thursday. He completed 68.2% of his passes for 345 yards and two touchdowns for a 106.7 passer rating, and that included just one pass to Loveland for a five-yard gain.</p><p>He threw 24 of his 44 passes to the trio of Swift, Odunze and Burden, who accounted for 228 of his yards. He threw to 10 receivers overall, including five passes to Roush (five catches for 31 yards) and four to Carlson (two for 30).</p><p>Williams targeted Loveland an average of 7.4 times over his first five games coming off a hamstring injury, and now that must be reallocated. The most profitable way to do that is turning to Odunze (15.7 yards per catch), Burden (12.9) and Swift (8.1).</p><p>At this point, more than halfway through Year 3, Williams should be able to navigate the attrition. Franchise quarterbacks are expected to get the job done no matter who they have at the skill positions, and that’s one of the first places teams trim spending when they have to shell out for a massive quarterback contract.</p><p>In this case, with Williams still playing on a cheap rookie deal, there’s still enough with which to work.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Black Friday still brings animal-loving volunteers to Chicago stores in the spirit of giving
entries.summary: <p>At Menards in Lincoln Park, the busiest aisle on Black Friday wasn't filled with shoppers hunting for electronics or holiday gifts. It was the one stacked with $1.50 blankets.</p><p>"You save big money at Menards," Marie Kukielka said. "I don't think I've ever been able to find a cheaper blanket."</p><p>Kulkielka is among volunteers from no-kill animal shelters like PAWS Chicago and Canines & Felines Rescue who cross paths once a year at Menards, filling shopping carts with blankets, toys and treats for animals awaiting adoption.</p><p>For the volunteers, the annual shopping trip is less about scoring deals for themselves than giving back.</p><p>Kukielka said she began volunteering for PAWS after moving to Chicago to attend DePaul University, just a few blocks from the shelter. She had been Black Friday shopping since childhood, but eventually decided to redirect that enthusiasm toward something more meaningful.</p><p>"I still want to go, but maybe I should channel that energy into something a little bit better than just buying stuff I don't need," she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure The haul was just the first stop of the day, with trips to Target, Aldi and HomeGoods still ahead. They purchased 75 towels, 500 toys, 100 blocks of cream cheese and 60 jars of peanut butter by the end of the shopping day. </p><p>The two have been making the Black Friday rounds for PAWS for over a decade. Kazimir said the crowds have thinned considerably since the pandemic, making it easier for them<b> </b>to get in and out quickly.</p><p>"It was a little more cutthroat back then," she said. "People would think our carts were part of the blanket bins and start taking blankets off."</p><p>Retail experts predicted more shoppers would head online this year than to stores this Black Friday according to <a class="Link" href="https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/183-million-consumers-expected-to-shop-during-thanksgiving-weekend" target="_blank" >a November survey </a>by the National Retail Federation, with 89 percent of shoppers expected to shop online. Overall, the number of shoppers over the Thanksgiving weekend was anticipated to fall by 2.2 percent from last year, the NRF report found.</p><p>But volunteer shoppers like Kazimir are still showing up in person. Now, she said, volunteers from other shelters have become familiar faces in the aisles, returning year after year to shop for those in need. </p><p>"I've seen other shelters coming for the blankets, can be a particularly busy time for the shelter, she said, as foster families travel and animals temporarily return to the adoption center. The organization is also preparing for its holiday adoption events.</p><p>PAWS raised more than $4,000 for this year's shopping trip, she said. Kukielka's bill totaled $1,375.22, but she saved $551.62 through the store's Black Friday discounts.</p><p>Behind them in the checkout line was Kim Riley and her mother, Nada, continuing a tradition of their own. For about 20 years, the mother-daughter duo have shopped Black Friday sales for Felines & Canines, an Edgewater-based no-kill animal shelter.</p><p>This year, they picked up 15 blankets and toys, accompanied by Ruby, a yellow Labrador puppy. She's training to become a therapy dog at Our Lady of Guadalupe School in the South Shore neighborhood, where Riley recently became principal.</p><p>For Riley, the early morning trip is worth it even on her days off.</p><p>"It's really the only reason, aside from going to work this early, that I get up this early to go, if we can help some animals," she said. "The point is to give. And if we have the means, we're happy to share it."</p><p>As shoppers increasingly turn to online deals and Black Friday crowds lose some of their traditional frenzy, the volunteers said the annual trips remain an opportunity to stretch donations and support Chicago's animal shelters.</p><p>"That's where everybody was today, all by the blankets," Riley said. entries.title: Heyworth beats Brown County in 1A title game to win its first football state championship
entries.summary: <p>NORMAL, IL —Jarrod Fulcher didn’t attend Heyworth High School because it was a football powerhouse. He just went to the high school in his hometown and worked hard with his friends to turn it into a football powerhouse.</p><p>“Two years ago Heyworth was 3-6,” Fulcher, an offensive and defensive lineman, said. “For years and years it was just a losing culture. What we just did switched to a winning culture.”</p><p>What Heyworth did was win the school’s first football state championship with a 19-16 win against Brown County in the Class 1A state title game on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/11/26/illinois-high-school-football-state-championship-scores-ihsa" >Friday</a> at ISU’s Hancock Stadium.</p><p>“Everyone here wanted to win,” Fulcher said. No one wanted to lose anymore. It was embarrassing. It was embarrassing to lose six games. Just our want and need to be better.”</p><p>Nate Godfrey, coach Scott Godfrey’s son, scored the game-winning touchdown with 7:32 to play. But the key score was Connor Kerr’s Class 1A state record 32-yard field goal midway through the third quarter.</p><p>“We had seen him on film, and knew he had a great leg,” Brown County coach Tom Little said. “That is a really nice piece that most 1A schools don’t have.”</p><p>The field goal put Heyworth (14-0) ahead 11-8. Brown County retook the lead late in the third quarter on Jack Sefton’s second touchdown run.</p><p>Braydon Laesch had 15 carries for 118 yards for Heyworth. Senior quarterback Caleb Troha finished with six carries for 85 yards, including a 19-yard TD run in the second quarter.</p><p>Troha found receiver Dane Strunk, who made an excellent catch at the one-yard line to set up the winning touchdown in the fourth quarter.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: 4 injured after sedan crashes into O'Hare shuttle bus
entries.summary: <p>A crash involving an O'Hare airport shuttle bus left four people injured Friday morning, according to Chicago police. </p><p>The crash happened around 6:05 a.m. when the shuttle bus was leaving Lot G and was struck by a white sedan going south on Bessie Coleman Drive, police said.</p><p>The 49-year-old sedan driver suffered injuries throughout the body and was taken to Lutheran General Hospital in critical condition, officials said. </p><p>The bus driver, a 40-year-old man, suffered an arm injury and was taken to Resurrection Hospital in good condition, police said. </p><p>A 46-year-old passenger suffered a leg injury and a second passenger, 44, suffered a cut to his head, authorities said. Both were taken to Resurrection and were in good condition. </p><p>Two additional bus passengers declined medical attention. </p>

entries.title: Revie Sorey, Bears guard who blocked for Payton and dedicated his life to helping at-risk kids, dies at 73
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p>Revie Sorey, the Chicago Bears offensive lineman who for nine seasons blocked for Walter Payton and went on to dedicate his life to helping Chicago's disadvantaged youth, died Thursday. He was 73.</p><p>Mr. Sorey was drafted by the Bears in 1975 and spent his entire NFL career with them. He wore number 69 and was an integral member of the Bears’ offensive line, playing 109 games between 1975 and 1983 and earning All-NFC honors.</p><p>Bears fans remember Mr. Sorey (his name is pronounced like it rhymes with "Stevie Story") as the 6-3, 280-pound graceful big man who helped clear a path on countless sweeps for Payton.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicago Sun-Times. | Bob Langer/Sun-Times archive</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"Everybody talks about his great infectious smile and how everybody he met became his buddy, his friend and how he went out of his way to make people feel special and guide people through their lives," said Anita Efron. She and her husband, Morton Efron, a Chicago attorney who represented Mr. Sorey after he graduated from college, were Mr. Sorey's closest friends and chosen family. </p><p>"I am getting literally hundreds of texts and emails from people who Revie helped. He just wanted to uplift people and show them how they could soar and be their best self," Anita Efron said. "Everybody has said that there's a connection with the Bears getting that win on Thanksgiving, the day he died, and, yeah, I think so, too."</p><p>Born in Brooklyn, New York, and raised in Bedford-Stuyvesant, he attended the University of Illinois, where he became a two-time All-Big Ten football selection and offensive captain.</p><p>Mr. Sorey, who played guard, was at Northwestern Memorial Hospital when he died, said Anita Efron.</p><p>"His heart just stopped. It was his time," she said.</p><p>The Efrons also released a statement Friday announcing Mr. Sorey's death and recounting details of his life.</p><p>Following his football career, Mr. Sorey devoted himself to creating opportunities for young people, eventually serving as director of educational services at Ada S. McKinley Community Services, a youth services organization at 1359 W. Washington Blvd.</p><p>He founded the Revie Sorey Trunk Scholarship Program with Anita Efron, ensuring that hundreds of first-generation college-bound Chicago students received trunks filled with everything from computers to bedding.</p><p>Mr. Sorey's wife, Suzy O’Malley-Sorey, died of pancreatic cancer in 2011. </p><p>Following her death, and with his own health beginning to fail, Mr. Sorey moved from his home in Glen Ellyn to the Efron's downtown home until a stroke in March 2012 left him unable to speak or walk and in need of around-the-clock care.</p><p>Mr. Sorey then moved into a room at the Warren Barr Pavilion rehabilitation facility on the North Side that the Efrons decorated with football memorabilia. Through lots of hard work and therapy, he regained limited use of speech. The Efrons and his old Bears teammates were frequent visitors.</p><p>A Sun-Times reporter was present in 2016 when ex-Bears teammates Tom Hicks, Brian Baschnagel and Bruce Herron, who served as unofficial team barber when he was with the Bears, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2014/12/20/18603034/ex-bear-revie-sorey-is-still-the-guard-of-attention" >stopped by to provide Mr. Sorey with a haircut and some company</a>.</p><p>“He nicknamed himself Dr. Rock Hollywood,” Hicks said then. Hicks met Mr. Sorey when they were freshmen at Illinois. “He was a riot. He dressed like Sly Stone. He drove a white Thunderbird with Dr. Rock Hollywood written on the back. It had a big aerial TV antenna on top that wasn’t attached to anything.</p><p>“I don’t know how much he paid in parking tickets. He was always parked illegally. He would wear a suit and carry a briefcase to class and then sleep through the lecture.”</p><p>In 2016, five years after his wife died, Mr. Sorey suffered additional heartache when his son, Trace Sorey, died in an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/10/18/18359510/trace-sorey-son-of-former-bears-guard-dead-at-24-in-drowning" target="_blank" >accidental drowning</a> at a pool in Los Angeles. He was 24.</p><p>"It was a horrible, just horrible," Anita Effron recalled.</p><p>Mr. Sorey, who'd been living most recently at The Clare, a senior living facility downtown, is also remembered for mentoring young athletes through the Revie Sorey All-Pro Football Camp, which he and Anita Efron ran for 27 years, teaching young people to grow both on and off the field.</p><p>He also hosted the Revie Sorey Racquetball Classic, raising funds for local charities while introducing the sport to a diverse audience.</p>

entries.title: Kenwood smashes Leo to win the Prep Bowl
entries.summary: <p>Colby Irvin wasn't in a mood to linger and celebrate after Kenwood won its first Prep Bowl title in dominant fashion Friday afternoon at Rockne Stadium.</p><p>Irvin is a junior starter on the offensive line for the Broncos, who set a Prep Bowl scoring record in a 60-16 win against Leo.</p><p>But he's also wing for the Kenwood basketball team, and he was in a hurry to get to a tournament game later Saturday against Rockford Jefferson at Rockford Auburn.</p><p>Irvin has a rare distinction: he's a Public League champion in two sports. He was a member of Kenwood's basketball champs as a freshman in 2025 and now he's not only won a football title but a Prep Bowl to boot.</p><p>"Winning two city championships as a young player feels good," Irvin said. "I can't even explain [it] right now, but I'm just happy. I love my team. None of this would be possible without them."</p><p>Some two-sport athletes might have skipped the Prep Bowl, which has lost much of its luster since the advent of the IHSA playoffs. But that thought didn't enter Irvin's mind, which didn't surprise Kenwood coach Chris Goffer.</p><p>"He was a captain as a junior," Goffer said. "Really a huge leader throughout the summertime and he's been itching to go play basketball but he stayed committed ... to football until we finished what we had to finish."</p><p>Junior quarterback Malachi Henigan accounted for four touchdowns for Kenwood (9-4), which led 39-8 at halftime. He ran eight times for 93 yards and two TDs, and was 6-of-11 passing for 94 yards and two scores. </p><p>Senior running back Jamarius Andrus ran 10 times for 79 yards and a TD and also scored on a fumble recovery. Senior receiver Lawrence Carr caught a TD pass and ran a free kick after a safety back for a touchdown.</p><p>Kenwood is the first Public League team to win the Prep Bowl since Simeon in 2022. The Catholic League leads 65-29 with two ties in a series that began in 1927 and has been played annually since 1933 except for 2020 when it was paused because of COVID.</p><p>One of the game's storylines in recent years is whether it will continue. Only two teams — Leo and DePaul Prep — opted into the Catholic League side of the bracket this year and Morgan Park principal Dan Kuzma pulled the Mustangs out of the Public League playoffs after the abrupt firing of coach Chris James. That's the first time a CPL team has opted out of the bracket.</p><p>Goffer is now a Prep Bowl champ as a coach and as a player with Mount Carmel in 2001. He hopes the tradition continues.</p><p>"I think when you keep the kids in the forefront, then the Prep Bowl stays alive," Goffer said. "It takes some of the coaches to really share the history of the Prep Bowl and the importance of it."</p><p>The series also has been a springboard for teams on the rise. St. Ignatius won the past two Prep Bowls and reached the Class 8A semifinals this season with many of the same players.</p><p>Rob Cunningham III ran for a TD for Leo (7-6), which played in its first Prep Bowl since 1956.</p><p>"It just sets the new standard about what the program is," Lions coach Theo Hopkins said. "We don't want to be ending our season [in the] last week of October, first week of November. We want to be playing later into the season."</p>

entries.title: Hunter Kaitschuck scores 5 TDs as Wilmington wins back-to-back 2A state championships
entries.summary: <p>NORMAL, IL — Wilmington's football team opened the season in the considerable shadow of last year’s Class 2A state championship squad, which coach Jeff Reents said featured the best offensive line he’d coached in his 26 years.</p><p>“Winning state last year definitely did not make things easier for us,” Wildcats senior Cooper Holman said. “There was that idea in the back of your head that if we don’t win state this year, we are a letdown.”</p><p>Holman and his teammates improved throughout the season as much as any team Reents has coached and capped it off on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/11/26/illinois-high-school-football-state-championship-scores-ihsa" >Friday</a> with a dominant 49-14 win against West Frankfort in the 2A state title game at ISU’s Hancock Stadium.</p><p>Wilmington has won four state titles in the past six seasons, so many guys are walking around town with state championship rings. But this is the first back-to-back title for the Wildcats.</p><p>“Yeah, maybe that will give us a little extra [status],” Holman said. “It was unreal to be part of that group last year.”</p><p>Wilmington (13-1) led 14-6 late in the second quarter when the big moment arrived. The Wildcats rarely throw the ball, but they surprised West Frankfort with a 42-yard touchdown pass from Brysen Meents to Holman.</p><p>Wilmington ran for 381 yards. Hunter Kaitschuck had 18 carries for 224 yards. He scored four rushing touchdowns and returned an interception for a touchdown, tying the 2A title game record with five touchdowns.</p><p>“I have to give all the credit to my offensive line,” Kaitschuck said. “None of that would be possible without their blocking. I want to give big thanks to them.”</p><p>Dane Van Duyne had 13 carries for 97 yards for the Wildcats.</p><p>“It took us a little while to find the right mixture of guys, and we found that during the season, obviously,” Reents said. “Our kids have confidence running the ball. They grow up with it.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a90000" entries.title: Big Ten's final four fight for two conference title game spots on Rivalry Saturday
entries.summary: <p>Look, it isn’t complicated.</p><p>After smacking Nebraska around 31-7 on Friday, all Iowa needs to clinch a spot in the final <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Big Ten</a> football championship game is for (a) both Indiana and Oregon to lose Saturday; (b) Indiana and UCLA to lose, and Oregon to win; (c) UCLA and Oregon to lose while Indiana, Michigan, Wisconsin and either Northwestern, Penn State or Rutgers win; (d) Indiana, Oregon and Wisconsin all to win, and UCLA to lose; or (e) Indiana, Oregon and UCLA all to lose.</p><p>See? Nothing could be simpler.</p><p>The path to Indianapolis for UCLA — alone in first place with only one conference loss — is even easier: just beat USC in the regular-season finale. Or, ahem, lose and hope (a) Indiana and Oregon both lose; (b) Oregon wins and Indiana loses; (c) Oregon loses, Indiana wins and either Minnesota or Ohio State wins; or (d) Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, Michigan State and Wisconsin all win, Oregon loses and — yes, one more “and” — UCLA ends up ahead of Iowa according to analytics metrics that I wouldn’t understand, let alone be able to explain, if I underwent intensive mathematics training for the next 47 years.</p><p>Indiana can play for the Big Ten title if it beats Purdue and (a) Oregon and UCLA both lose or (b) Minnesota and Oregon both win, and UCLA loses. Not that much to it.</p><p>Oregon gets there if it beats Washington and (a) UCLA wins or (b) Indiana wins and UCLA loses. What is this, kindergarten?</p><p>Good news, in the sense that things have become a bit more streamlined: Iowa’s win eliminated both Ohio State — the preseason No. 1-ranked team in the land — and USC from contention.</p><p>So we are down to a not-so-fabulous four, given how much the Big Ten has struggled this season. Oregon, which has the cleanest path to Indy, has become the betting favorite to win there on Dec. 5. UCLA, the conference’s top team in the playoff rankings at No. 9, is suddenly facing a five-alarm fire at quarterback, its fate in peril. Defending national champ Indiana isn’t dead yet — for Indy or for the playoff — while Iowa, pretty unexpectedly, by now is playing the best football of any team in the conference.</p><p>It’s a lot to take in, if I'm being honest.</p><h3><b>Week 13 picks</b></h3><p><i>All games are Saturday. My picks to cover are listed first, with CFP rankings in effect.</i></p><p><b>No. 4 Notre Dame (-24½) vs. Syracuse </b>(11 a.m., ABC 7, 780-AM): I might’ve gone the other way had former Golden Domer Steve Angeli been at quarterback for the Orange; unfortunately, he got hurt last weekend and will miss this chance to shine. Backup Malachi Nelson is at his fourth school and sitting on 12 career touchdown passes with 12 interceptions and no discernible ability to run the ball. Easy pickings for the Irish, 38-7.</p><p><b>Northwestern (-2½) vs. Illinois </b>(11:30 a.m., BTN, 890-AM, 720-AM): The Wildcats’ season was derailed by the loss of QB Aidan Chiles after a truly outstanding eight-game stretch. The Illini are a completely different team with QB Katin Houser than they are without him, but his status is up in the air. In this much doubt, I’m taking the overall healthier home team by a field goal.</p><p><b>No. 15 USC (-6½) at No. 9 UCLA </b>(2:30 p.m., CBS 2): Is there a theme this week? You bet there is. We don’t know if Bruins QB Ty Dieffenbach will be able to play. Without him, the offense has been a disaster. The Trojans have Jayden Maiava’s NFL-caliber arm and something to play for — knocking their crosstown rivals out of the playoff. Trojans, 24-14.</p><p><b>Auburn (+15½) at No. 6 Alabama </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): The Tigers won at Georgia, hung in there all game at Tennessee and, in their last road game, massacred Mississippi State by 32. Can they win the Iron Bowl in Tuscaloosa for the first time since Cam Newton was taking the college football world by storm? Probably not, but I’m tipping my helmet to them for a pretty good season. Crimson Tide by single digits.</p><p><b>No. 12 Oregon (-14) vs. No. 24 Washington </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5): The Ducks will still have everything to play for when kickoff arrives, so I’m expecting a fast start. Quack Attack, 34-17.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 14 Indiana (-22) vs. Purdue </b>(6 p.m., FS1): Curt Cignetti isn’t sure how he’s going to will his Hoosiers back into the playoff, but if bludgeoning the rival Boilermakers with the Old Oaken Bucket will help, let’s just say he won't hesitate.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>Michigan (+10½) at No. 21 Ohio State </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32): Wouldn’t it be a trip if, by the end of this one, Buckeyes coach Ryan Day were on an even hotter seat than Wolverines counterpart Kyle Whittingham? Nah, can’t happen … or can it? Maize and Blue, 16-13.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>5-2 straight-up, 5-2 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>61-26 straight-up, 52-35 against the spread.</p>

entries.title: Chicago's winter overnight parking ban returns Tuesday night — with higher fees
entries.summary: <p>Chicago drivers could wake up to at least $360 in fees if they park on the wrong streets overnight this winter. The city's annual overnight parking ban begins Tuesday, restricting parking on 107 miles of major streets.</p><p>The ban is enforced from 3 a.m. to 7 a.m. every day from Dec. 1 through April 1, according to the Department of Streets and Sanitation.</p><p>Vehicles parked in violation of the ban will be towed, and the cost is up significantly from last winter. Owners will face a minimum towing fee of $250, up from $150 last year, a $60 ticket and a $50 daily storage fee, which has doubled from $25.</p><p>The fees had remained unchanged for more than a decade before January of this year, when the department first increased them. The higher rates now also apply to the winter overnight parking ban.</p><p>The city tows an average of 60 to 65 vehicles per night throughout the winter season for violations of the overnight parking ban, the department added.</p><p>Vehicles are towed to Pound 2 at 10301 S. Doty Ave. or Pound 6 at 701 N. Sacramento.</p><p>The overnight ban is separate from the city's 2-inch snow parking ban, which applies to another 500 miles of main streets. That restriction can take effect whenever at least two inches of snow accumulate on the street, regardless of the time of day or date.</p><p>Drivers parked on affected streets during a snowstorm could receive a ticket or have their vehicles relocated to make way for snow-clearing operations.</p><p>The city has permanently posted signs across streets affected by the overnight ban. The Streets and Sanitation Department also distributes flyers on parked cars before the restrictions begin.</p><p>The restrictions were introduced after major snowstorms in 1967 and 1979 brought Chicago traffic to a standstill.</p><p>Drivers can check whether their street is affected by viewing the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/streets/provdrs/traffic/svcs/winter-snow-parking-restrictions.html#docaccess-cb7d3abbbbd58f90e3493cb936e45f68" target="_blank" ><u>city’s parking ban map</u></a>. To check if your car was towed, visit <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/streets/supp_info/chicagoshovels.html" target="_blank" >chicagoshovels.org</a>, or call 311.</p>

entries.title: Patrick Kane lands back on injured reserve, but Blackhawks hope injury can be 'managed'
entries.summary: <p><b>Patrick Kane</b> landed on injured reserve for the second time in a month Friday, leaving the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ lineup more short-handed than it already was.</p><p>Kane blocked a shot off his right foot or ankle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/26/blackhawks-kraken-sweep-trip-blocked-shots-roman-kantserov" target="_blank" >Wednesday</a> against the Kraken and will miss at least three games.</p><p>Coach <b>Jeff Blashill</b> said the ‘‘best-case scenario’’ is that Kane will return Thursday at the Predators, which is the soonest he will be eligible to be activated.</p><p>‘‘We anticipate this is something that can be managed and he can be back sooner than later,’’ Blashill said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Patrick Kane’s blocked shot: <a href="https://t.co/VAI73NkwwD">pic.twitter.com/VAI73NkwwD</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2126443630521188440?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 27, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Still, it’s brutal timing for the Hawks and Kane. The Hawks faced the Rangers on Friday without five key players: Kane, <b>Connor Bedard</b> (shoulder surgery), <b>Tyler Bertuzzi</b> (illness), <b>Bowen Byram</b> (unspecified upper-body) and <b>Wyatt Kaiser</b> (suspension).</p><p>Kane had been excellent since a brief IR stint this month, too. He was playing easily his best hockey of the season, developing strong chemistry with linemates <b>Frank Nazar</b> and <b>Oliver Moore</b> and contributing to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/26/blackhawks-power-play-penalty-kill-improvement" target="_blank" >red-hot power play</a>.</p><p>He extended his point streak to six games with an assist Wednesday not long before the blocked shot, which was instrumental in helping the Hawks close out that victory.</p><p>The Hawks called up wingers <b>Dillon Boucher</b> and <b>Landon Slaggert</b> from Rockford of the AHL to fill out their lineup (while sending down center <b>Dominic Toninato</b>). They will get Kaiser back Sunday against the Wild.</p><p><b>Alex Vlasic</b> and <b>Ian Cole</b> served as alternate captains with the entire leadership group — Bedard, Kane and Bertuzzi — out.</p><h3>Byram non-update</h3><p>Blashill said Byram, who hasn’t played since Oct. 13, still is skating, but there’s still no ‘‘definitive timeline’’ for his return.</p><p>It must be clarified that Byram isn’t sitting out because his baby girls were, as of Nov. 14, still in a neonatal intensive-care unit. His injury and his babies’ health are unrelated.</p><p>He easily could have taken a personal leave, such as former Sabres teammate <b>Rasmus Dahlin</b> did last season, if he needed time off for family reasons.</p><h3>Bedard’s timeline</h3><p>After the surgery on Bedard’s right shoulder Monday, the Hawks issued almost word-for-word the same statement they issued after his surgery in July, estimating he’ll miss four months.</p><p>Four months from Monday is March 23. If Bedard returns that day, he will end up missing 53 games and will come back for the last 10 of the season.</p><p>But it seems likely he’ll return sooner than that, considering he came back a little more than three months after his surgery in July. If he returns Feb. 26, for example, he could make 23 appearances before the season ends.</p><h3>Rockford report</h3><p>Forward <b>Nick Lardis</b> likely would have been called up Friday if he hadn’t just suffered an injury that’s expected to cost him multiple weeks.</p><p>Lardis’ second pro season isn’t going as hoped, considering he now has been injured twice with Rockford — where he has seven points in 10 games — after a slow start with the Hawks got him sent down the AHL.</p><p>Forward <b>Marek Vanacker</b>, a first-round pick in 2024, is also off to a slow start in his first pro season with Rockford. He has five points in 20 games.</p><p>The Hawks’ other two notable first-year pro forwards in Rockford, <b>AJ Spellacy</b> (five points) and <b>Sacha Boisvert</b> (one point), have been disappointing, too.</p><p>Rockford’s brightest spot has been <b>Gavin Hayes</b>, a third-year pro forward with 19 points in 20 games. He has positioned himself to get an NHL look at some point.</p>

entries.title: Man shot in head multiple times during Chicago Lawn gunfight
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot in the head multiple times Friday afternoon while standing outside in Chicago Lawn.</p><p>The man, 56, was in the 5900 block of South Richmond Street in the southwest side neighborhood on Friday at around 1 p.m., standing near a vehicle, Chicago police said. </p><p>An unknown number of armed people fired shots at each other, police said. The 56-year-old man, in the vicinity when shots were fired, was hit in the head multiple times. </p><p>He was taken to a hospital in critical condition. The gunmen fled in an "unknown direction," police said. </p>

entries.title: Bears' defense on alert, 'pissed off,' after shaky performance in 39-35 win over Lions on Thanksgiving
entries.summary: <p>One of the most refreshing aspects of how <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> are run under coach Ben Johnson is that every assessment of how they’re playing is rooted in reality and based strictly on the facts.</p><p>There’s never any effort to paint a rosier picture. If anything, Johnson errs on the side of looking for what’s wrong, even in victory, and spent all last season pointing out his team’s flaws even as it went 11-6 and won the NFC North.</p><p>It’s the only way to improve.</p><p>Newcomer Jeffery Simmons is fully on board with that approach, and after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/26/bears-draft-dream-comes-true-as-qb-caleb-williams-wr-rome-odunze-lead-39-35-win-over-lions" >the Bears’ stunning 39-35 last-second win over the Lions</a> on Thanksgiving, his attention went to defensive lapses that must be urgently addressed if the Bears are going to chase a championship.</p><p>“It’s a lot of frustration, because as a defense, I don’t like the way they made plays,” he said. “We’ve got to enjoy this one, but when you look ahead and think about our ultimate goal, we have to play better.</p><p>“I’m happy we got a win, but I’m also pissed off that we didn’t play up to our standards.”</p><p>It’s worth noting that the Bears were tangling with the NFL’s No. 1 offense, a Lions team stacked with weapons and a surgical quarterback. It’s also worth noting, though, that the Bears will face plenty more powerful offenses down the stretch, including the Jaguars on Dec. 6, and in the playoffs.</p><p>While big-picture concerns about their defense subsided after Simmons’ arrival by trade last month, the Bears still looked shaky against the run leading up to Thursday in Detroit. Sure enough, facing NFL leading rusher Jahmyr Gibbs, they allowed 7.9 yards per carry and 246 overall — nearly double their previous season-worst rushing total.</p><p>Gibbs, who ran for an NFL season-high 205 yards and three touchdowns, was one play away from icing the game and preventing Bears quarterback Caleb Williams’ winning touchdown pass to Rome Odunze.</p><p>Lions quarterback Jared Goff threw him a screen pass on fourth-and-four at the Bears’ 33-yard line with 2:17 remaining, and Gibbs had a one-on-one opportunity against linebacker T.J. Edwards to get the first down. Edwards came up big with a direct hit — “I couldn’t sit there and let him move around,” he said — to stop him three yards short, setting up the Bears’ final drive.</p><p>If there was one heroic play on defense, that was it.</p><p>Yet even Edwards, who went to a Super Bowl with the Eagles and knows precisely what a championship-caliber defense looks like, didn’t use that tackle to cover up the Bears’ many defensive missteps.</p><p>“There were some plays I wish we had back,” he said, thinking specifically about the Lions’ 71-yard touchdown drive in a little over a minute shortly before halftime. “I was pissed.”</p><p>That’s how Johnson felt, too, as the game seemed to be slipping away from the Bears.</p><p>Williams and the offense clawed back into it multiple times, but the defense couldn’t get a stop. Over a stretch from late in the second quarter to midway through the fourth, the Lions scored on four consecutive possessions, culminating with Gibbs’ 70-yard touchdown run in which the Bears didn’t get near him until he already was 30 yards into it, to lead 35-24 with 8:20 remaining.</p><p>Simmons said at one point, Johnson screamed at the defense, “Just get me the [expletive] ball back.”</p><p>The Bears ended up allowing 549 yards of total offense, which was the third-highest in the league this season and the most against the Bears since 1982.</p><p>Facing arguably the best offensive line in the league, the Bears had their first game this season without getting a sack. That allowed Goff to pick apart their secondary for 313 yards and a touchdown. His only blemish was a late interception by safety Dillon Thieneman, which tanked Goff’s passer rating from 105.4 to 93.9.</p><p>The Jaguars’ Trevor Lawrence is capable of doing that. So is former MVP Josh Allen of the Bills, whom the Bears visit next month. They’ll see the Packers’ Jordan Love and Goff again before the end of the regular season.</p><p>There were signs of this coming, too.</p><p>The defense saved the Bears in ugly wins over the Buccaneers and Saints the previous two games, but struggled against the run in both. The Bucs ran for 126 yards at 4.5 per carry, and the Saints put up 120 at a 5.5 average.</p><p>The Bears now sit 16th in total defense and 13th against the run, though the latter of those statistics is skewed in their favor because, thanks to mostly playing with a lead and controlling time of possession, they’ve faced the fourth-fewest run plays. They’re allowing five per carry, which is third-worst.</p><p>The defense came through at key moments and, by definition, did enough for the Bears to win in Detroit, but that’s not the point. That’s never Johnson’s perspective. In the long run, process proves more important than result, and giving up 35 points and 549 yards is far from a sound formula to keep winning.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Caleb Williams' comeback proves Bears 'still got that tool in our arsenal'
entries.summary: <p>Receiver Rome Odunze sat on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> bench awaiting a replay review that would confirm the most consequential catch of his NFL career, a six-yard toe-tap touchdown in back right corner of the Ford Field end zone with three seconds to play Thursday.</p><p>Once the call was confirmed, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/27/where-will-bears-qb-caleb-williams-look-now-that-top-tes-cole-kmet-colston-loveland-are-injured" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a>, the quarterback who rallied the Bears, found Odunze on the bench to celebrate.</p><p>“That’s why I’m ‘Ice,’ baby,” Williams said, while an elated Odunze smacked him on the chest.</p><p>Williams got his “Iceman” nickname last year for his ability to stay cool with the Bears behind in the final minutes of games. Really, though, he was Superman — and, all too often, Clark Kent in the first three quarters.</p><p>Amazingly, though, Williams didn’t need the cape at any point this season. Were Thursday a movie, the quarterback would have walked into his closet, dusted it off and tried it on to see if it still fit.</p><p>Because Williams has been better throughout games this season, his heroics hadn’t been needed late in them. Amazingly, the quarterback hadn’t played a snap when the Bears trailed in the final four minutes of any game this season — until Thursday.</p><p>Last year, though, Williams played a whopping 57 such snaps over nine games, more than half the Bears’ regular-season schedule. He had a passer rating of 98.1 during that span, and the Bears went 6-3. In the playoffs, Williams had a 117.4 passer rating when trailing in the final four minutes of regulation, throwing touchdowns to beat the Packers and force overtime in an eventual loss to the Rams.</p><p>The closest Williams has come to a gotta-have-it situation this year came in Week 9, when he took possession in a tied game and marched the Bears to a game-winning field goal at the gun against the Buccaneers.</p><p>He’s given the Bears exactly what coach Ben Johnson said he wanted this offseason — more consistent play throughout the game. Thursday, though, he proved that he can still be the “Iceman.”</p><p>“I think he’s got that nickname for a reason,” Johnson said. “They believe in him. I think we have a veteran O-line. A lot of those guys have been there and done that, so they kind of – they’re all good. Then our skill guys, they’re just young and hungry, and they’re excited to go out there and make plays. …</p><p>“It’s a little bit unique because we haven’t had one of these [comeback wins] this year — not quite like this at least — and so it’s good to know we still got that tool in our arsenal.”</p><p>That’s critical in a league that, as the rest of the Thanksgiving slate proved, is often decided by who plays well as the clock ticks down.</p><p>The Bears wouldn’t have had a chance to win the game, though, had Williams not hunted the matchup he wanted midway through the fourth quarter. Down 11 with 8:20 to go, Williams zipped down the field, finding Luther Burden and Odunze for back-to-back 15-yard gains before heaving an out-and-up down the right sideline. Odunze sprinted past a stumbling Rock Ya-Sin — the same cornerback in coverage for the game-winner — for a 41-yard touchdown.</p><p>“I've learned this over my career so far,” Wlliams said. “Yes, you go through reads … But late in games, you go to matchups. Late in games, you go to your guys. And I think that was just one of those moments that I felt good. I told Rome that I was going to keep coming back to him.”</p><p>Then, after T.J. Edwards’ spectacular tackle of Jahmyr Gibbs on fourth-and-four, came the 13-play, 68-yard game-winner.</p><p>“[Williams] wants the ball in his hands, and he wants to make plays,” Odunze said. “We cater to that. Down the stretch, he remained poised, knowing that we had a game-winning drive on the line.”</p><p>Johnson, Williams and the Bears calmly bled the clock as they marched down the field — to the frustration of the Lions.</p><p>“It sucks to sit there on the sideline and watch them do that,” Lions quarterback Jared Goff said. “You tip your cap to how well they played and how they roared back there in the fourth quarter.”</p><p>Williams hadn’t needed earlier this year. Entering Thursday, the Bears had led through three quarters in all six games that Williams both started and finished. Their cushion was staggeringly large, too — the Bears scored 72 more points than their six opponents through three quarters.</p><p>They trailed through three quarters Thursday, but believed they could come back.</p><p>“It’s a lot of confidence in their quarterback more than anything else,” Johnson said.</p>
